books.title: The Steam Engine
books.art_why: The book covers 1700s and 1800s events from before photographs, so drawings fit.

pages.text: An Invention That Changed the World For thousands of years, people used their muscles for work. They also used animals to help them. In the 1700s, the invention of the steam engine changed everything. People began to make fewer goods by hand. Instead, they used machines. Many of those machines were powered by steam.
pages.brief: In a workshop, people use their muscles and animals to help with work. Nearby, in the 1700s, people stand beside machines powered by steam instead of making goods only by hand, showing the change the steam engine brought.

pages.text: What Is Steam? Have you ever watched someone boil water in a pot on the stove? Sometimes you can see a little cloud above the pot. That’s steam. It can only be seen when it hits cooler air. Steam is a gas. People make steam do work by boiling water. They heat up the water in a gigantic pot called a boiler. They make the boiler hot by burning fuel, such as coal. Burning coal becomes hotter than the top of a stove—a lot hotter! The heat boils the water and makes steam. Steam takes up more room than liquid water. As the steam expands, it pushes the moveable parts of a machine. The movement of those parts creates power.
pages.brief: A person watches a pot of boiling water on a stove, with a small cloud of steam above it. Beside them, a large boiler burns coal, and expanding steam pushes the moving parts of a machine to create power.

pages.text: The First Real Steam Engines Almost 300 years ago, in 1712, Thomas Newcomen built a steam engine. Others had built steam engines, but Newcomen’s was the first to work really well. He used his steam engine to run a water pump, which pumped water out of coal mines. Miners could then reach more coal. The engine had one problem. It needed a large amount of coal to do a small amount of work.
pages.brief: At a coal mine, Thomas Newcomen stands beside his 1712 steam engine, which runs a water pump. Miners watch as water is pumped out of the mine so they can reach more coal, while a large pile of coal shows the engine’s fuel.

pages.text: Steam Engine Improvements In the 1760s, Scotsman James Watt improved Newcomen’s engine. He made the machine work with less coal. Watt also made other kinds of steam engines. He made one called the rotary (circular) steam engine. It could run all kinds of machines. This invention was one event that led to the Industrial Revolution, also known as the Age of Steam. The Age of Steam brought new ways to do work and new ways for people and goods to travel.
pages.brief: James Watt stands beside an improved steam engine that burns less coal. A circular rotary steam engine turns machinery in a factory, while people and goods travel nearby, showing the new ways of work and travel during the Age of Steam.

pages.text: High-Pressure Steam Engines At the beginning of the Age of Steam, Watt’s steam engines used low- pressure steam. His steam engines were big, and they operated, or worked, slowly. Watt knew he could make smaller and faster steam engines. But he would have to use higher-pressure steam. He was against that idea. Higher pressure could cause a boiler to explode. An explosion could injure or kill people.
pages.brief: James Watt stands beside a large, slow low-pressure steam engine. He looks worried as he imagines a high-pressure boiler exploding, with steam bursting out, because an explosion could injure or kill people and he opposed the idea.

pages.text: Many inventors saw the danger of high- pressure steam. They built high-pressure steam engines anyway. They thought that smaller engines could be used to do more things. In the early 1800s, Richard Trevithick (trev-ITH-ik) built a high-pressure steam engine in England. High-pressure steam engines soon became common. They could be used to power trains.
pages.brief: In England in the early 1800s, Richard Trevithick stands beside a compact high-pressure steam engine. Other inventors also build smaller high-pressure engines despite the danger, and a train powered by high-pressure steam waits nearby, since these engines could soon power trains.

pages.text: Steam-Powered Transportation Trevithick built one of the first steam locomotives, or trains, in 1804. It hauled coal at a factory. Other people also built train engines. Soon these engines were pulling long lines of cars with passengers or goods. Steam engines helped railroads spread across the world.
pages.brief: Richard Trevithick’s early steam locomotive pulls cars loaded with coal at a factory in 1804. Nearby, other steam train engines pull long lines of cars carrying passengers and goods along spreading railroad tracks across the world.

pages.text: In the early 1800s, ships also began to use steam. Some sailed on the oceans. New Yorker Robert Fulton built the first moneymaking river steamboat in 1807. By the mid-1800s, beautiful steamboats traveled up and down American rivers. River steamboats presented the danger that James Watt had warned about. Steam explosions sometimes happened with locomotives, but they were common with steamboats. Many people were injured or killed in steamboat accidents.
pages.brief: Robert Fulton’s moneymaking river steamboat travels on an American river in 1807. By the mid-1800s, beautiful steamboats carry passengers up and down rivers, while steam explosions on crowded steamboats show the danger that injured or killed many people.

pages.text: One of the worst disasters in American history took place on April 27, 1865. The boiler on the crowded steamboat Sultana exploded. The ship burned. More than 1,700 people died.
pages.brief: On April 27, 1865, the crowded steamboat Sultana burns on a river after its boiler explodes. Dark smoke and flames rise from the ship as the disaster unfolds, and more than 1,700 people die in one of the worst disasters in American history.

pages.text: The Age of Steam Draws to a Close By the early 1900s, people had found ways to replace steam power. In factories, electricity now ran most machines. Electric engines did not produce steam or smoke. Electric engines made subways and streetcars easy for everyday use. It became easier to travel around a city. The diesel engine also doomed the steam engine. It ran better and could go farther faster. Steam locomotives ran in the United States until the 1960s. By then, almost all locomotives had diesel engines.
pages.brief: In a factory, electric machines run without steam or smoke, and an electric streetcar and subway make city travel easier. A diesel locomotive stands beside an old steam locomotive, showing how diesel engines ran better and farther faster, while steam locomotives ran in the United States until the 1960s.

pages.text: Modern Uses of Steam Although the Age of Steam is long over, steam is still important. For instance, power plants use it to produce electricity. It powers your lights and your television. How Much Coal per Family Power plants burn thousands of pounds of coal every year to provide power for just one U.S. household. Appliance Pounds of Coal.
pages.brief: A power plant burns coal to heat water and produce steam for electricity. The electricity powers lights and a television in a nearby U.S. household, while a large amount of coal is shown as the fuel needed to provide power for just one family.

pages.text: Some people believe there is still a need for steam power. Steam power, they say, costs less than diesel fuel for trains. Steam power can also be generated using solar panels, which do not use fossil fuels like coal to make electricity. That makes steam power better for the environment than it is now. Steam power is useful and will probably have a place in the modern world.
pages.brief: People stand beside solar panels that generate steam power without fossil fuels, and near a modern steam train that costs less to run than diesel. In the background, a diesel train waits, while the people look hopeful that cleaner steam power will have a place in the modern world.

books.title: Summer Olympic Events
books.art_why: Keyword check suggests drawing; the book mixes historic origins with sports action.

pages.text: Summer Olympic Events.
pages.brief: A wide stadium filled with summer sunlight, with athletes from different sports standing together on the track: a runner, a swimmer, a gymnast and a cyclist, all ready for the Summer Olympic Games.

pages.text: The Summer Olympic Games The modern Summer Olympic Games began in 1894. They were inspired by athletic competitions held in ancient Greece. The Games are intended to promote understanding and friendship among people from all countries. The Summer Olympics are held every four years. Each Olympics is held in a different city around the world. Athletes compete in hundreds of events. They try their best to win gold, silver, or bronze medals for their home countries. Summer Olympics Host Cities Montreal, Canada 1976 Athens, Greece 2004 Moscow, Russia 1980 Beijing, China 2008 Los Angeles, California 1984 London, England 2012 Seoul, South Korea 1988 Rio de Janeiro, Brazil 2016 Barcelona, Spain 1992 Tokyo, Japan 2021* Atlanta, Georgia 1996 Paris, France 2024 Los Angeles, California 2028 Sydney, Australia 2000.
pages.brief: A large stadium holds athletes from many countries, with runners, jumpers and throwers competing before a crowd. Nearby, a globe suggests the Games moving to different host cities every four years, while gold, silver and bronze medals gleam for the athletes who try their best.

pages.text: The Olympic Torch The Summer Olympics start with an opening ceremony. The ceremony usually includes a parade of the athletes. An important part of the ceremony is the lighting of the Olympic flame by a person carrying the Olympic torch.
pages.brief: An opening ceremony fills a stadium with a parade of athletes walking together in colorful teams. In the center, a person carries the Olympic torch and lowers it to light the Olympic flame, while spectators watch from the stands.

pages.text: The torch is lit in Greece several months before the start of the games. It is then carried to the host city by a series of runners. It arrives at the Olympic stadium on the opening day of the games. By this time, it has been handed off from one runner to the next many times during its long journey. At the opening ceremony, the final runner enters the stadium carrying the torch. They use it to light the Olympic flame. The Olympic flame burns throughout the Olympics. It is not put out until the closing ceremony.
pages.brief: A relay of runners carries the Olympic torch across roads and hills toward the host stadium. In Greece, the torch is first lit; months later, the final runner enters the stadium, carries it around the track and lights the Olympic flame, which burns until the closing ceremony.

pages.text: Events The Summer Games include team sports such as basketball, soccer, volleyball, and field hockey. They also include many individual events. Let’s look at some of the events.
pages.brief: A busy sports field shows team events: basketball players leap toward a hoop, soccer players chase a ball, volleyball players reach for a net, and field hockey players carry sticks. Around them, individual athletes train, showing some of the many Summer Olympic events.

pages.text: Water Sports Water sports include water polo, diving, and swimming. Some of the swimming races are short, and swimmers swim only two lengths of the pool. Other races are longer. They sometimes include more than one swimmer in a relay.
pages.brief: At a bright pool, water polo players pass a ball through splashing water while divers leap from high boards. Swimmers race in short events over two lengths of the pool, and in longer relay races several swimmers take turns, each one diving in to continue the race.

pages.text: Many swimming races allow swimmers to use only one kind of stroke. But in the freestyle event, swimmers can choose the stroke they want to use. The breaststroke, backstroke, and the butterfly are all used in different races.
pages.brief: In lanes of blue water, swimmers use different strokes: one swims the breaststroke, another the backstroke, and another the butterfly. In a freestyle race, a swimmer chooses the stroke they want, cutting through the water with strong arms and steady kicks.

pages.text: In diving events, divers jump from high above the water. Divers do twists, flips, and turns while in the air. They get points for the difficulty of the dive and how small a splash they make when they hit the water.
pages.brief: High above a swimming pool, a diver jumps from a platform and performs twists, flips and turns in the air. Judges watch closely, ready to award points for the dive's difficulty and for how small a splash the diver makes when hitting the water.

pages.text: Track and Field Track and field events include running, throwing, and jumping competitions. The marathon is the longest running event. It is over 42 kilometers (26 mi) long. The shortest races are called dashes.
pages.brief: On a track and field ground, runners line up for a short dash, while a marathon runner races far along the road. Nearby, athletes practice throwing and jumping. The marathon is the longest running event, more than forty-two kilometers, and the dashes are the shortest races.

pages.text: Runners often train for the Olympic Games by running in locations high in the mountains. This training helps their bodies become better at delivering oxygen to their muscles to create energy.
pages.brief: High in the mountains, runners train on winding paths, breathing the thin air. Their bodies work hard to deliver oxygen to their muscles, helping them create energy. Below, a stadium track waits, where their mountain training may help them race better at the Olympic Games.

pages.text: In throwing events, the objective is to throw a hammer, discus, javelin, or shot put as far as possible. Athletes competing in these events must be very strong.
pages.brief: Strong athletes take their places for throwing events. One spins to throw a hammer, another hurls a discus, a third launches a javelin, and a fourth pushes a shot put. Each athlete tries to send the object as far as possible across the field.

pages.text: In jumping events, athletes are judged on the height or distance of their jumps. In the high jump, athletes leap over a bar. The bar is raised higher until only one person can jump it. In the long jump, athletes leap as far as they can. In the pole vault, athletes use a pole to help them leap over a very high bar.
pages.brief: At jumping events, an athlete leaps over a high-jump bar while another jumps as far as possible in the long jump. A pole-vaulter uses a long pole to lift over a very high bar. The high-jump bar rises higher and higher until only one person can clear it.

pages.text: Gymnastics Gymnasts leap, flip, and twirl through the air. They demonstrate their timing, balance, flexibility, strength, and skill. Some popular events include the rings, balance beam and the pommel horse. In the balance beam event, they must turn and flip on the narrow beam.
pages.brief: Gymnasts leap, flip and twirl through the air. One swings on the rings, another balances on the narrow balance beam and turns and flips there, and another grips the pommel horse. Their routines show timing, balance, flexibility, strength and skill.

pages.text: Fencing Olympic fencers duel with practice swords. They score points by touching their opponents with their swords on different parts of the body. Fencers wear protective masks and clothing and use special swords so that the competition is safe. Fencers are allowed to move forward and backward as they fight, but they can only move a little from side to side. Fencers use three different kinds of swords.
pages.brief: Two fencers duel with practice swords, wearing protective masks and clothing. They score points by touching each other on different parts of the body. They move forward and backward as they fight, only a little from side to side, and they use three different kinds of swords.

pages.text: Pentathlon One event created specifically for the Olympics is the pentathlon. The founder of the modern Games, Baron Pierre de Coubertin, created this event. He was inspired by the pentathlon in the Ancient Olympics. The name pentathlon comes from the Greek words for five and contest.
pages.brief: Baron Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Games, stands beside athletes of the pentathlon. He created this Olympic event, inspired by the pentathlon of the Ancient Olympics. The name comes from Greek words for five and contest, linking the five different challenges.

pages.text: The pentathlon is based on an imaginary scenario of a soldier who is trapped behind enemy lines. The athlete must ride a horse, shoot targets with a pistol, fight with a sword, run, and swim. The competitor with the best total score in all five events wins. Both men and women compete in the pentathlon.
pages.brief: A pentathlete moves through five challenges like a soldier trapped behind enemy lines: riding a horse, shooting targets with a pistol, fighting with a sword, running and swimming. The competitor with the best total score in all five events wins, and both men and women compete.

pages.text: Event Categories The Summer Olympics include more than thirty sports with hundreds of events. More events can be added at every Olympics. Summer Olympic Sports Aquatics Archery A thletics (Track and Field) Badminton Baseball/Softball Basketball Boxing Breaking Canoe Cricket Cycling Equestrian Fencing Flag Football Football (Soccer) Golf Gymnastics Handball Hockey Judo Karate Lacrosse Modern Pentathlon Rowing Rugby Sevens Sailing Shooting Skateboarding Sport Climbing Squash Surfing Table Tennis Taekwondo Tennis Trampoline Triathlon Volleyball Weightlifting Wrestling.
pages.brief: A wide array of Summer Olympic athletes fill a stadium: rowers, archers, boxers, cyclists, gymnasts, swimmers and many more. They represent more than thirty sports and hundreds of events, with new events able to be added at every Olympics. Together they show the huge variety of the Summer Games.

books.title: Sonia Sotomayor Joins the Supreme Court
books.art_why: Sonia Sotomayor and the Supreme Court are real and can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: A Big Dream When she was a young girl, Sonia Sotomayor dreamed of becoming a detective. Doctors told her when she was eight that she had Type 1 diabetes. It was a big change. Sonia had to learn to take good care of herself because this is a serious condition. Sonia’s dreams also changed. She wanted to become a lawyer.
pages.brief: A young Sonia Sotomayor imagines herself as a detective. At age eight, a doctor tells her she has Type 1 diabetes and explains that she must take good care of herself. Later, she imagines herself as a lawyer.

pages.text: Sonia’s parents had moved to New York from Puerto Rico. Sonia’s father died when she was nine. Her mother worked hard to support Sonia and her brother. Sonia tried to be the best student she could be. She studied, made good grades, and won many awards. She won scholarships, or money for school, to attend Princeton University and then Yale Law School. She was an excellent student at both schools.
pages.brief: Sonia’s parents moved from Puerto Rico to New York. After her father dies when she is nine, her mother works hard to support Sonia and her brother. Sonia studies, earns good grades, wins awards and scholarships, and attends Princeton University and Yale Law School.

pages.text: The Dream Comes True After graduating from law school, Sotomayor got her first job as a lawyer. Her dream had come true. After several years as a lawyer, her dream changed again. She wanted to become a judge. Her dream came true in 1991.
pages.brief: After law school, Sonia Sotomayor begins her first job as a lawyer, and her dream comes true. After several years, she wants to become a judge. In 1991, her new dream comes true.

pages.text: In May 2009, President Barack Obama had to choose a new justice for the U.S. Supreme Court. One of the justices, David H. Souter, was retiring. The president announced that Judge Sotomayor was his choice to replace Justice Souter. The president said she had done a great job as a judge and would be a wise justice. Do You Know? Justices of the U.S. Supreme Court are very important. They decide if laws follow the U.S. Constitution. The Constitution is the country’s set of rules and laws that protect our rights. The nine justices of the Supreme Court make decisions that affect many people.
pages.brief: President Barack Obama stands with Judge Sonia Sotomayor as he announces she is his choice for the U.S. Supreme Court. Justice David H. Souter is shown retiring. Nearby, nine Supreme Court justices sit together, representing the court that decides if laws follow the Constitution.

pages.text: Picking a New Justice Presidents often choose a justice who agrees with them on important ideas. All U.S. Supreme Court justices have worked as lawyers. Many justices have not been judges in other courts, as Sotomayor has. A justice can be any age. The youngest justice was thirty-two when chosen. The oldest was sixty-five. Presidents often choose a younger person so he or she can work on the court for many years. Sotomayor was fifty-five when President Obama chose her.
pages.brief: A president thinks about choosing a Supreme Court justice who agrees with his important ideas. The scene shows that all justices have worked as lawyers and that justices can be any age. Sonia Sotomayor is shown at age fifty-five, when President Obama chose her.

pages.text: The Supreme Court is over two hundred years old. For most of that time, all of the justices on the court have been white men. Yet the justices make decisions that affect all kinds of people in different areas of the country. Some presidents now try to make the court more representative of the country. Thurgood Marshall joined the court as its first Black justice in 1967. Sandra Day O’Connor joined the court as its first female justice in 1981.
pages.brief: An older Supreme Court scene shows many white male justices. The court is more than two hundred years old. Thurgood Marshall is shown joining as the first Black justice in 1967, and Sandra Day O’Connor is shown joining as the first female justice in 1981.

pages.text: Finding the Right Person President Obama, like other presidents before him, asked for help to find the best justice. Lawyers and advisers to the president made a list of people who would make good justices. They checked to make sure the people on the list were fair and followed the law. Sonia Sotomayor was on the list. She had been a lawyer and judge for many years. She would be the third woman ever to be a Supreme Court justice. Sotomayor would join Ruth Bader Ginsburg, the second woman on the court. Judge Sotomayor would be the first Latina and the first person with diabetes to be chosen as a justice.
pages.brief: President Obama’s lawyers and advisers make a list of fair people who follow the law. Sonia Sotomayor is on the list after many years as a lawyer and judge. She is shown as the third woman ever, joining Ruth Bader Ginsburg, and as the first Latina and first person with diabetes chosen as a justice.

pages.text: After President Obama talked to Judge Sotomayor, he picked her to be a justice. However, the president couldn’t decide who became a justice on his own. A majority of the U.S. Senate had to agree with his choice. A Change in the Supreme Court A justice retires or dies. The president chooses a new justice. A justice serves as long as he or she wants or is able. The Judiciary Committee investigates the choice. The new justice takes the oath. The committee advises the Senate. The Senate votes “ No.” The Senate votes “ Yes.”
pages.brief: President Obama talks with Judge Sonia Sotomayor and picks her. A sequence shows a justice retiring or dying, a president choosing a new justice, a committee investigating the choice, and the new justice taking an oath. Senators then vote, with both a No vote and a Yes vote shown.

pages.text: The Judiciary Committee A group of senators called the Judiciary Committee investigated Judge Sotomayor. She answered the senators’ questions about decisions she had made as a judge. She talked about things she had said in speeches. Judge Sotomayor explained how she would be fair when deciding cases in the future. The committee reported its findings to the rest of the Senate. The president would have to choose someone else if the Senate did not confirm Judge Sotomayor.
pages.brief: Judge Sonia Sotomayor sits before the Judiciary Committee. She answers senators’ questions about her decisions as a judge and things she said in speeches, and she explains how she would be fair in future cases. The committee reports its findings to the rest of the Senate.

pages.text: The Senate Votes Some people who disagreed with President Obama’s ideas also disagreed with choosing Judge Sotomayor. But when the Senate voted on August 6, 2009, the majority voted to confirm Judge Sotomayor. Two days later, Sonia Sotomayor took an oath, or made a promise, to follow the Constitution. She was now the 111th justice of the U.S. Supreme Court.
pages.brief: Senators vote on August 6, 2009, and the majority confirms Judge Sonia Sotomayor. Two days later, she takes an oath to follow the Constitution. She is shown as the 111th justice of the U.S. Supreme Court.

pages.text: The Job of the New Justice Supreme Court Justice Sonia Sotomayor has an office in the Supreme Court Building. She had to hire people to work in her office. She also had to learn the rules of the Supreme Court, just as you would learn the rules at a new school. Justice Sotomayor’s main job now is to listen to cases that are brought to the Supreme Court and make wise decisions.
pages.brief: Justice Sonia Sotomayor has an office in the Supreme Court Building. She hires people to work in her office and learns the rules of the Supreme Court. Her main job is to listen to cases brought to the court and make wise decisions.

pages.text: Conclusion Justice Sotomayor has made many dreams in her life come true. Being a justice is a very important job. Most presidents only get to choose one or two Supreme Court justices during their time in office. It is a very important decision. Justice Sotomayor tries to be the best justice she can be. She helps make decisions that affect all Americans!
pages.brief: Justice Sonia Sotomayor is shown at work, having made many dreams come true. The scene suggests how important it is for a president to choose a Supreme Court justice, since most presidents choose only one or two. She tries to be the best justice she can be for all Americans.

books.title: Sinkhole Science
books.art_why: Real sinkholes, cities and natural landforms can be photographed; no named famous person is featured.

pages.text: Two Huge Holes For a few weeks in 2007, people in a neighborhood of Guatemala City felt the ground tremble and shake. No one knew what was causing it. Then on February 23, a huge hole suddenly opened in the street. A dozen houses tumbled into the pit, and several lives were lost. The hole was more than 330 feet (100 m) deep— deep enough to swallow two Statues of Liberty.
pages.brief: In a Guatemala City neighborhood in 2007, the ground trembles before a huge hole suddenly opens in the street on February 23. A dozen houses tumble into the deep pit. People in the neighborhood are nearby as the sinkhole opens, deeper than the surrounding buildings.

pages.text: In 2010, it happened again, fifteen blocks from the first hole. This time, the hole swallowed a three-story clothing factory and left another gaping chasm in a major intersection. Miraculously, no one was injured. Sinkholes happen all over the world, in the middle of cities and in the middle of nowhere. Though sinkholes take years to form, each time a new sinkhole opens up in the earth, it takes people by surprise. What Causes Sinkholes? The ground we stand on feels solid. Underground, however, a lot is happening. Water trickles and flows, slowly eroding rocks and soil. This creates underground spaces. These result in sinkholes. Sinkholes don’t happen just anywhere, though. Most natural sinkholes form where there are certain kinds of soft bedrock. Bedrock is a layer of underground rock. The ground above it and on the surface is called the overburden. 5 Sinkhole Science.
pages.brief: Fifteen blocks from the first hole, a 2010 sinkhole swallows a three-story clothing factory and leaves a gaping chasm in a major intersection. Below the surface, water trickles through soil and rock, eroding underground spaces beneath a layer of overburden.

pages.text: Rain or underground water drips and flows into this bedrock and erodes it. This creates open spaces such as underground caves or caverns. Over time, these spaces get bigger. Eventually, the overburden may slowly drop down to form a sinkhole. Sometimes, though, sinkholes can open suddenly and swallow buildings, cars, and people. Two Types There are two main types of sinkholes. The first is a cover-subsidence sinkhole ( subside means to sink or settle). A cover-subsidence sinkhole forms when water wears a space in the underground bedrock. The overburden above the bedrock then shifts downward. Most sinkholes of this kind form slowly and may measure only a few yards across. The overburden may contain a lot of sand that easily slides into the underground space. These sinkholes often create a bowl shape on the surface. They may become ponds or wetlands if water has no way to drain out.
pages.brief: Underground, water drips and flows into soft bedrock, eroding open caves and caverns. Over time the spaces grow larger. The overburden above may slowly drop to form a bowl-shaped cover-subsidence sinkhole. Sand slides downward, and a surface bowl collects water, becoming a pond or wetland.

pages.text: Cover-Subsidence Sinkhole 1 Water dissolves some types of bedrock. The result is an underground cavity. 2 Sediments from above spill into the bedrock cavity. As a result, the surface begins to sink. 3 Slow downward erosion creates a surface bowl. If water collects here, the bowl may become a pond or wetland. The second type is a cover-collapse sinkhole. This sinkhole forms when a space gets bigger and bigger under the surface. The overburden gets thinner as dirt, sand, and other sediment fall into the space. The ground around this kind of sinkhole may contain a lot of sticky clay. Clay helps hold the overburden together. Without warning, though, the surface may collapse into the underground space. 7 Sinkhole Science.
pages.brief: A cover-subsidence sinkhole appears in three stages: water dissolves bedrock and creates an underground cavity; sediments from above spill into the cavity; slow downward erosion makes a surface bowl. If water collects in the bowl, it may become a pond or wetland. The second type, cover-collapse, is introduced.

pages.text: Areas that get a lot of sinkholes usually have bedrock made of karst. Karst is made of any type of rock that dissolves easily, such as limestone. Karst can also be formed of gypsum, dolomite, salt, or other minerals and rocks. Karst has many holes and cracks that water can flow into. When rainwater soaks into the earth, it picks up a mild acid from leaves and plants. The mild acid dissolves karst. This helps create the underground spaces that cause natural sinkholes.
pages.brief: An area with karst bedrock is shown, full of holes and cracks where water can flow. Rainwater soaks into the earth, picks up a mild acid from leaves and plants, and dissolves limestone, gypsum, dolomite, salt, or other minerals. This creates the underground spaces that cause natural sinkholes.

pages.text: Cover-Collapse Sinkhole 9 Sinkhole Science.
pages.brief: Beneath the surface, a large underground cavity grows under a thin overburden of dirt and sticky clay. The surface collapses suddenly into the space below without warning, leaving a steep-sided cover-collapse sinkhole.

pages.text: Amazing Natural Sinkholes Sinkholes fascinate geologists. They study them to learn more about how water and earth affect each other. Here are three amazing natural sinkholes from around the world. The Qattara Depression is the world’s largest natural sinkhole. It is located in Egypt and is 137 miles (220 km) long and 75 miles (120 km) wide. That is twice the area of the state of Rhode Island.
pages.brief: The Qattara Depression in Egypt stretches across a vast desert landscape as the world’s largest natural sinkhole. It measures 137 miles long and 75 miles wide, twice the area of Rhode Island. Geologists study natural sinkholes to learn how water and earth affect each other.

pages.text: China’s Xiaozhai Tiankeng is considered the deepest sinkhole in the world. More than 2,165 feet (660 m) deep, this sinkhole could swallow a 200-story skyscraper. The Sarisarinama sinkholes in Venezuela were discovered in 1961. Scientists have discovered plants and animals inside that are found nowhere else. Sinkholes Caused by Humans Some sinkholes result from underground construction. In cities, tunnels and pipes crisscross under many buildings and streets. If those pipes get old and worn out, they can collapse, allowing liquid to escape and eat away at the ground. Eventually, the pavement caves in. Work crews must check these underground spaces regularly to make sure they are solid. If a sinkhole forms in a city it can do a lot of damage, as in Guatemala City, where leaking pipes may have triggered the gaping holes in the city streets. 11 Sinkhole Science.
pages.brief: China’s Xiaozhai Tiankeng appears as an immense, deep sinkhole, more than 2,165 feet deep, deep enough to swallow a 200-story skyscraper. In Venezuela, the Sarisarinama sinkholes hold plants and animals found nowhere else. In a city, old pipes under streets collapse, liquid escapes, and pavement caves in.

pages.text: Underground mines can also cause sinkholes. Near one Russian city, underground water filled an old mine. The bedrock of salt began dissolving. In 1986, a huge sinkhole opened up. It grew to 780 feet (238 m) deep and covered more area than 25 football fields. It is still growing, and new sinkholes are opening up. Hundreds of people have had to leave their homes. To be safe, the entire city may need to move. Some geologists argue that holes caused by human activity shouldn’t be called sinkholes because true sinkholes result from natural processes. Garbage In, Garbage Out People sometimes treat sinkholes like garbage dumps. They will throw in junk, trash, even animal waste. This is a terrible idea. Many sinkholes drain into underground water sources. This is the same water that people drink. It is the water that farmers use to water their crops. The result is pollution in our food and drinking water.
pages.brief: Near a Russian city, water fills an old underground mine and dissolves salt bedrock. In 1986 a huge sinkhole opens, growing 780 feet deep and wider than 25 football fields. It is still growing, forcing hundreds of people to leave their homes. Trash and animal waste thrown into sinkholes can pollute drinking water.

pages.text: Dealing with Sinkholes Predicting where natural sinkholes will form is tricky. The erosion that creates them is usually hidden underground. The type of bedrock is the most important factor in whether or not sinkholes form. Areas with soft bedrock that also get heavy rains are at even greater risk. The rainwater adds weight to the overburden. The draining water can also speed up underground erosion. Where Sinkholes Sink 13 Sinkhole Science.
pages.brief: Geologists assess where natural sinkholes may form. Soft bedrock is the most important factor. Areas with soft bedrock and heavy rains face greater risk because rainwater adds weight to the overburden and draining water speeds underground erosion. Predicting sinkholes is tricky since the erosion is hidden underground.

pages.text: Tilting trees or signposts can be early clues that the ground is shifting. Growing cracks in walls and sidewalks can also warn that a sinkhole is getting ready to cause trouble. If a sinkhole forms under a house, homeowners can pour tons of dirt and concrete into the hole. This is called grouting. The goal is to plug the hole. Sometimes, though, the dirt and concrete just disappear into the underground space. Another method uses steel rods. These long, strong rods are pushed into solid bedrock deep underground. The rods are then joined to the base of the house. This helps keep the building stable and safe.
pages.brief: Tilting trees and signposts stand as early clues that the ground is shifting. Cracks grow in walls and sidewalks. Under a house, workers pour tons of dirt and concrete into a sinkhole to plug it, called grouting. Long steel rods are pushed into solid bedrock and joined to the house’s base to keep it stable.

pages.text: Conclusion Sinkholes can be destructive, but they are rarely dangerous. In some places, they are even beautiful. In parts of Mexico, for instance, sinkholes form lovely pools full of cool, clean water. Sinkholes are also interesting to study. They show water’s powerful effects on soil and rock. Even on solid ground, amazing things are happening beneath our feet. 15 Sinkhole Science.
pages.brief: In parts of Mexico, sinkholes form lovely pools of cool, clean water. The conclusion shows sinkholes as destructive but rarely dangerous, and sometimes beautiful. They are interesting to study because they show water’s powerful effects on soil and rock, even beneath solid ground.

books.title: Park Rangers
books.art_why: Real park rangers, parks, wildlife, and places can be photographed.

pages.text: Park Rangers.
pages.brief: A park ranger stands on a scenic trail in a national park, looking out over mountains and trees. The ranger carries a backpack and appears ready to guide visitors through the outdoors and care for the park.

pages.text: What’s It Like to Be a Park Ranger? Imagine being a park ranger. Picture yourself leading visitors to a beautiful hidden waterfall. Think about walking people step-by-step through an exciting battle from history. Imagine holding a turtle for schoolkids to touch. Imagine skiing into a snowy forest to save a hurt hiker.
pages.brief: A park ranger leads visitors toward a hidden waterfall, while another ranger walks people through a historic battle scene and a third holds a turtle for schoolchildren. In the distance, a ranger skis into a snowy forest to help a hurt hiker.

pages.text: Being a park ranger is a lot of work. Rangers work long hours. They work nights and weekends. They might hike for miles in a single day. They face wild animals and wild weather. Still, most rangers say it’s the best job in the world. Ranger Gear Rangers wear uniforms so visitors know who they are. They carry gear that helps them do their outdoor job. A typical ranger needs: • hiking boots • bear spray* * Bear spray is high- powered pepper spray. If a wild animal attacks, bear spray can stop it.
pages.brief: A park ranger in uniform hikes for miles along a rough trail, wearing hiking boots and carrying bear spray. Storm clouds gather and a wild animal watches from the brush as the ranger works late into the evening.

pages.text: Where Do Rangers Work? Park rangers work in national or state parks. Some parks are beautiful natural areas, such as the Grand Canyon and Yellowstone. Others are important places from history. Many parks include museums and public buildings. Some include memorials, which help us remember an event or a person who died.
pages.brief: A park ranger stands before the Grand Canyon, with Yellowstone’s geysers in the distance. Nearby are a history museum, a public building, and a memorial honoring an event or a person who died, showing the many places rangers serve.

pages.text: Parks are special places set aside for the future, but people visit parks today. They hike, ski, and fish in parks. They see beautiful art. They walk on beaches and rest near waterfalls. Park rangers work to keep all the visitors safe. Rangers also teach people about the park and how to save it for the future.
pages.brief: Visitors hike, ski, and fish in a broad park landscape. Others walk on a beach, rest beside a waterfall, and look at beautiful art. A park ranger watches over them and gestures toward the park, teaching visitors how to protect it.

pages.text: What Do Rangers Do? Park rangers do many different jobs. Some rangers teach the public. At Carlsbad Caverns in New Mexico, rangers teach people about bats while millions of them fly out of a cave. At George Washington’s birthplace in Virginia, rangers show how the Washington family ate dinner in the 1730s. At Alcatraz Island in California, rangers tell how some men escaped from the famous prison.
pages.brief: At Carlsbad Caverns, a ranger teaches visitors as millions of bats stream from a cave. At George Washington’s birthplace, a ranger shows a 1730s family dinner. At Alcatraz, a ranger tells visitors about men who escaped the famous prison.

pages.text: Some rangers work with scientists and other experts. In the Everglades, rangers track Florida panthers. They make sure these endangered animals are safe and healthy. In Banff National Park in Alberta, Canada, rangers keep track of wildfires set to keep the forest healthy. Park rangers also help protect parks. In Navajo National Monument in Arizona, rangers make sure visitors don’t damage Native American ruins. On Cape Hatteras in North Carolina, rangers keep people from stepping on bird nests. Endangered birds lay their eggs on the beach.
pages.brief: In the Everglades, a ranger and scientist track a Florida panther. In Banff, rangers monitor a wildfire set to keep the forest healthy. At Navajo National Monument, a ranger makes sure visitors do not damage Native American ruins, and at Cape Hatteras a ranger keeps people from stepping on bird nests.

pages.text: Leader of the Pack Not everyone who works for the National Park Service is a ranger. Take biologist Doug Smith, who studies animals in Yellowstone National Park. “Everyone confuses biologists with rangers,” Smith says. In the early days of the Park Service, rangers did biology and everything else. Now, he says, “They're really involved with taking care of people.” Smith’s focus is more wolves than people. He came to Yellowstone in 1994 to help restore wolves to the park. Today, there are eleven packs in the park and 85–90 wolves. “In the park, it is clear that our mission is to restore natural systems, to bring nature back to the way it was before we messed it up,” Smith says. “So we did it, and we're doing it, and we're trying to understand it.”
pages.brief: Biologist Doug Smith stands in Yellowstone National Park, watching wolves spread across the grassy landscape. A park ranger listens nearby as Smith gestures toward several wolf packs and other scientists take notes on the animals.

pages.text: Other park rangers keep visitors safe. In the Great Smoky Mountains in Tennessee, rangers sign in every hiker. They make sure everyone comes home safely. If a hiker goes missing, rangers search the mountains. If a hiker is sick or hurt, rangers may need to fly the person out. Saving people can be dangerous. Rangers face flash floods, crumbling cliffs, and wild animals. In fact, park rangers have one of the riskiest jobs in the world!
pages.brief: In the Great Smoky Mountains, a ranger signs in hikers at a trailhead. Another ranger searches the mountains for a missing hiker, while a helicopter flies a sick or hurt person out. Nearby are flash-flood water, crumbling cliffs, and wild animals.

pages.text: What Do Rangers Need to Know? Rangers in different parks know about different things. At Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park, a ranger shows visitors how lava created the mountains, caves, and sea cliffs. A history expert at the Statue of Liberty tells what the statue means to people moving to the United States. Musicians at the New Orleans Jazz Park play music the city is famous for.
pages.brief: At Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park, a ranger points out lava-formed mountains, caves, and sea cliffs. At the Statue of Liberty, a history expert speaks to visitors. At the New Orleans Jazz Park, musicians play the city’s famous music for a crowd.

pages.text: Even rangers working in the same park are experts on different subjects. One ranger in Glacier National Park describes how glaciers shaped its beautiful valleys. An animal expert leads scientists to the park’s mountain goats. Another expert talks about the stars in the big, dark Montana sky. A ranger who knows first aid helps a hurt hiker.
pages.brief: In Glacier National Park, one ranger describes how glaciers shaped the valleys. An animal expert leads scientists toward mountain goats, another expert points out stars in the dark Montana sky, and a ranger with first aid skills helps a hurt hiker.

pages.text: Can I Be a Park Ranger? Does being a park ranger sound like fun? You can start by becoming a park volunteer. Volunteers do many of the same jobs as rangers. They learn about what goes on inside a park. Most rangers go to college. Some study history or science, while others study the wild lands and how people use them.
pages.brief: A park volunteer works alongside a ranger inside a park, learning the same outdoor jobs. Nearby, college students study history, science, wild lands, and how people use parks, preparing for a future ranger career one day.

pages.text: Many people want to be park rangers. To get the job, you must show that you’re a hard worker and a good leader. If you love nature and history, and you want to help preserve it, you might make a great ranger! pages.brief: A young person looks at a wide map of Canada, the United States, Hawaii, and Mexico showing many park locations. In the background, rangers work in forests, historic sites, and along coastlines, showing the many places rangers preserve.

books.title: European Castles
books.art_why: The Middle Ages predate photography, so the scenes must be drawn.

pages.text: E uropean uropean European Castles C astles astles.
pages.brief: A European castle is shown as the central subject, with a strong outer wall and multiple towers rising above it. The view is from outside, showing the castle as a large fortified home and stronghold, with no people visible.

pages.text: E uropean uropean C astles astles.
pages.brief: Another view of the same European castle, seen from a different angle so its towers, walls, and gateways are clear. The castle sits as a large fortified building, with a solid outer wall and several high towers, and no people are shown.

pages.text: What Is a Castle? During the Middle Ages, many castles were built across Europe. The castles were made to protect people from their enemies. They had thick, tall walls and watchtowers where guards stood watch over the castle. The people who owned the castles were the nobles. However, they were not the only people living in the castles. The people who served and protected the nobility also lived within the castle walls. The nobles not only owned and lived in the castle, they also owned much of the land stretching beyond the castle. They helped the monarch control the land.
pages.brief: A medieval castle with thick, tall walls and a watchtower rises over its courtyard. A guard stands in the watchtower, while a noble family and the servants who protect and serve them move within the walls. Beyond the castle, open land stretches out under the sky.

pages.text: Living outside the castle was another class of people called commoners. They were the craftspeople and farmers who lived in small towns and villages and on farms not far from the castle. In exchange for living on the noble’s land, the commoners farmed the land and paid taxes to support the castle.
pages.brief: Outside the castle walls, commoners live in a small village and on nearby farms. Farmers work the land, craftspeople make goods in simple workshops, and the castle stands in the distance. Some villagers carry produce and payments toward the noble’s land.

pages.text: The First Castles The first type of castle was called a mott- and-bailey. The mott was a high mound of dirt with a wooden tower built upon it. A wooden fence, called a palisade, was built out from the mott. The palisade formed a wall surrounding the bailey, or the yard, that held the kitchen, hall, stables, and other buildings belonging to the noble.
pages.brief: A mott-and-bailey castle stands on a high mound of dirt, topped by a wooden tower. A wooden palisade fence runs out from the mound and surrounds the bailey yard, where a kitchen, hall, stables, and other wooden buildings belong to the noble.

pages.text: Later, castles had stone motts or towers. Many of these castles also featured moats. Moats were ditches, often filled with water, that surrounded the castle. As time passed, castles were built with bigger towers and walls. They became larger, with more rooms and passages. They came to look more and more like the large castles we see today. These castles were well built and have withstood the test of time.
pages.brief: A later stone castle rises with larger towers and thicker walls, surrounded by a water-filled moat. Inside, many rooms and passages are suggested through open doorways and windows. The strong stone structure stands solid and lasting, unlike the earlier wooden castle.

pages.text: Outside the Castle Newly built castles were painted with a mixture of lime and water. This mixture gave the castle walls a fresh, clean coat of white. For this reason, the mixture was called whitewash. Every castle’s design was different. Still, they had many of the same features. Most had towers or turrets, and many castles had an inner and an outer wall. Many also had a very strong building in the center of the castle. This building was called a keep.
pages.brief: The outside of a newly built castle shows whitewashed walls, towers, turrets, an inner wall, an outer wall, and a strong central keep. The design is specific to this castle, yet it shares these common features with many others.

pages.text: Many castles were built in places that made them easier to defend. Many were built in the middle of lakes or on jagged hilltops and cliffs. This made it hard for attackers to reach the castle. The walls were often more than 3 meters (10 ft.) thick. The walls were topped with crenelations that gave them a sawtooth look. This design protected archers from enemy arrows. It also made it more difficult to climb over the walls. The primary entrance was through the main gate. But often there were smaller gates around the castle’s walls. These smaller gates were used for extra traffic or for deliveries to the kitchens.
pages.brief: A castle sits on a jagged hilltop beside deep water, with very thick walls topped by sawtooth crenellations. An archer stands behind the battlements, while attackers would struggle to climb. The main gate is large, and smaller gates open along the castle walls for extra traffic and kitchen deliveries.

pages.text: Castles had many windows to let light in. This meant that fewer candles and torches would be needed to light the rooms and halls. Windows near the ground were extremely narrow so that attackers could not climb through them. Since windows high above the ground were difficult to reach, they could be bigger. Most of these larger windows had shutters to keep out bad weather and often had bars to keep invaders out. The roofs and floors were made of hard wood. Many castles had cellars that were used to store food and wine. After the Middle Ages, dungeons were built in castle cellars. These dungeons were used to house prisoners.
pages.brief: A castle wall shows narrow windows near the ground and larger high windows with shutters and bars, letting in light. Inside, hard wooden roofs and floors are visible above a cellar storing food and wine. A separate dungeon area in the cellar holds prisoners, added after the Middle Ages.

pages.text: Inside the Castle Castles weren’t designed just to be defended. They were also designed to make life comfortable for the nobles. One of the most important places in a castle was the Great Hall. It was where meals, entertainment, and feasts were held. It was also where everyone gathered to talk or hold meetings. The kitchens were separated from the Great Hall by long passageways. Some kitchens were outside in another building to avoid the risk of the castles’ wooden roofs catching fire. This meant that food for medieval feasts could arrive at the tables cold or wet with rain!
pages.brief: Inside the castle, nobles gather in a large Great Hall for a feast, with tables set for meals, entertainment, and meetings. Long passageways connect to kitchens; one kitchen stands outside in another building to reduce fire risk, so food on the outdoor path can become cold or wet in rain.

pages.text: A castle had enough rooms to house the noble and their extended family. Visitors probably slept on straw mattresses in the Great Hall after the tables had been cleared away. Most castles had spiral staircases. They wound upward in a clockwise direction. They were built this way to slow down invaders by making it difficult to fight in the stairwells.
pages.brief: A castle has many rooms for a noble and their extended family. In the Great Hall, tables are cleared away and visitors lie on straw mattresses to sleep. A spiral staircase winds upward in a clockwise direction, built to slow invaders and make fighting in the stairwell difficult.

pages.text: Built for Defense One of the most important things to consider in castle design was defense. A castle usually had two surrounding walls. The inner wall was taller than the outer one. Archers standing on the inner wall could fire their arrows over the defenders on the shorter wall. It also made it easier for those on the taller wall to defend against attackers who had reached the lower outer wall. The two sets of gates on these walls often opened at opposite ends of the castle. This forced invaders to circle around the inside of the outer wall to find the other gate. While looking for the second gate, invaders could be hit by the castle guards’ arrows.
pages.brief: A castle shows two surrounding walls, with the inner wall taller than the outer one. Archers on the inner wall fire over defenders on the shorter outer wall, while the two gates sit at opposite ends. Invaders must circle inside the outer wall, where castle guards can hit them with arrows.

pages.text: Between the castle walls were the outer and inner wards. The outer ward was filled with shops and houses. The inner ward was where the food and weapons were stored, the knights stayed, and water wells were dug. In the center of the castle was a separate building called the keep. It was here that the nobility lived. It was the safest part of the castle and the hardest to enter. It was designed so that if the rest of the castle were captured, the nobles could still be defended.
pages.brief: Between the castle walls are the outer and inner wards. The outer ward holds shops and houses, while the inner ward stores food and weapons, houses knights, and contains water wells. In the center stands the keep, where the nobility live; it is the safest, hardest place to enter and can still defend them if the rest of the castle falls.

pages.text: People In and Around the Castle During the Middle Ages, life revolved around the church. People believed that God gave the kings and queens the power to rule. The church had at least as much power as the monarch. It represented the authority that gave the monarch the right to rule.
pages.brief: A medieval church stands at the center of daily life, with townspeople gathered around it. A king and queen are shown receiving their right to rule, while church leaders stand with equal power and authority. The people believe God gives the monarch the power to govern.

pages.text: Under the king and queen were several other classes of people. The highest class was the nobles. They paid the monarch a tax for the privilege to control land in the kingdom. The knights also ranked high in the kingdom. Below the knights were the merchants and artisans. And below them were craftspeople and peasants, such as blacksmiths and farmers. All these people paid taxes to the nobles. Some of them were allowed to hold land.
pages.brief: A king and queen sit above a line of medieval people arranged by class. Nobles pay a tax for land, knights stand near them, merchants and artisans come below, and craftspeople and peasants such as blacksmiths and farmers are lower still. Some of these people hold land and pay taxes to the nobles.

pages.text: The lowest class was the peasants. They had to remain on the land where they were born. Peasants did not own land. These farmers had to give much of what they produced to the monarch and the landowner. A peasant’s life was tough. They paid high rents to the nobles and were hit worst during times of hunger, war, and illness. Many rebellions occurred due to the peasants’ unhappiness with the nobles, but these were almost always shut down by the ruling class.
pages.brief: Peasants work the land where they were born, giving much of what they produce to the monarch and landowner. They own no land and pay high rents, while hunger, war, and illness make their lives hard. A group of unhappy peasants gathers in rebellion, but armed rulers move in to shut it down.

pages.text: Castles and War Castles were the targets of many long- running wars. Sometimes, walls were built around entire towns. The peasants would defend this town wall for as long as they could. If the town wall were overrun, then knights would defend the outer wall of the castle. If that fell, then the inner wall was defended. And lastly, the center building, or keep, that housed the nobles was defended.
pages.brief: A town surrounded by walls is attacked during a long war. Peasants defend the town wall, while behind them knights stand ready at the castle’s outer wall. If that wall falls, the inner wall is defended, and lastly the central keep where the nobles shelter is protected.

pages.text: Defending the castle was not easy. Enemies used many weapons to try to take over a castle. They used large battering rams to hammer away at the castle’s walls and gates. They used weapons called catapults to hurl rocks, debris, and even dead animals or people over the walls. Giant slingshot-like weapons called trebuchets were also used to hurl objects over the walls. And to discourage the castle defenders from rushing out of the castle to attack them, the attackers used giant crossbows mounted on carts.
pages.brief: Attackers surround a castle with siege weapons. A large battering ram hammers at the walls and gate, catapults hurl rocks, debris, and even dead animals or people over the walls, and trebuchets fling objects from a distance. Giant crossbows mounted on carts aim at the castle to discourage defenders from rushing out.

pages.text: Many methods were used to keep attackers from entering a castle. Holes were cut into the floors of arches above the castle entrance. Defenders poured burning sand or tar on anyone trying to batter down the gates. Newer castles replaced arrow slits with keyhole-shaped windows where cannons could be placed.
pages.brief: Defenders use the castle entrance to stop attackers. Holes are cut into the floor of the arch above the gate, and burning sand or tar is poured down on anyone battering the gates. On newer castles, keyhole-shaped windows replace arrow slits so cannons can be placed there.

pages.text: The moat, often filled with water, surrounded the castle. It was difficult to tunnel under a moat, and attackers could not wade across the deep water. There is a myth that crocodiles were placed in some moats. Some moats did have eels and other kinds of fish in them for food, but there were no crocodiles.
pages.brief: A deep water-filled moat surrounds the castle, making it hard for attackers to tunnel under it or wade across. In the water, eels and other fish swim as food for the castle. No crocodiles are present, though a myth says some moats held them.

pages.text: Often it was not possible to break into a well-built and well-defended castle. So the attackers would simply wait for the castle’s residents to run out of food or water.
pages.brief: A well-built, well-defended castle stands strong while attackers camp outside. Unable to break in, the attackers simply wait, watching the gates and walls for the castle’s residents to run out of food or water. The castle remains sealed and difficult to capture.

pages.text: The ruins of a castle in Scotland Around the 1600s, castles became less and less popular. They were no longer easy to defend because of the use of heavy cannons in warfare. The nobles also wanted more comfortable and open places to live. Still, many castles stand today as a reminder of an age gone by.
pages.brief: The stone ruins of a castle in Scotland stand on open ground, with broken walls and towers showing the passage of time. Around the 1600s, castles became less popular because heavy cannons made them harder to defend, and nobles wanted more comfortable, open homes. Many castles still stand today as reminders of an age gone by.

books.title: Sharks
books.art_why: Sharks and ocean life are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: Sharks are fish But unlike most other fish, sharks have no bones Shark skeletons are made of cartilage, which is the same material that gives human ears their shape Unlike most fish, sharks have rough skin The closest relatives of sharks are skates and rays, which are flat, diamond-shaped fish Sharks have an excellent sense of smell and are able to see well in poor light They are especially sensitive to the sounds and movements of injured animals Sharks can even sense the tiny bits of electricity that are produced by all living things Sharks can sense fish buried under the sand on the ocean floor.
pages.brief: A shark swims through the ocean, its rough skin visible, while flat, diamond-shaped skates and rays glide nearby. Near the sandy ocean floor, the shark senses small fish buried under the sand. Its skeleton is made of cartilage.

pages.text: Size variation in sharks and comparison with human Physical Description Sharks come in many sizes Some dogfish sharks are only a few inches long The whale shark is the largest fish in the world Most sharks have powerful, streamlined bodies to help them catch their prey Most large sharks have few natural enemies Many sharks are protected by camouflage patterns that help them blend in with their surroundings They are dark on the top and pale on the bottom Some sharks, called swell sharks, protect themselves from attack by puffing up their bodies with air or water This behavior makes them appear larger and helps to keep predators away Camouflage patterns help sharks sneak up on their prey.
pages.brief: A great white shark, a whale shark, and a pale catshark appear beside a human for size comparison. A small dogfish shark swims nearby. One shark has dark upper skin and a pale underside. A swell shark puffs up with water, appearing larger.

pages.text: Sharks swim by swinging their tails from side to side Sharks use their fins to steer, turn, and keep their balance The dorsal fin, which sharks use to keep upright, sometimes sticks out above the water Catching sight of a shark’s dorsal fin is often the first warning people have that a shark is nearby Eating The shape of a shark’s teeth depends on the kind of food it eats Most sharks have many rows of teeth When one tooth breaks off, another one moves up to take its place Sharks’ teeth break off easily A shark may wear out and regrow a thousand teeth during its lifetime. Do You Know?
pages.brief: A shark swims by swinging its tail from side to side. Its fins steer and keep balance, and its dorsal fin sticks out above the water surface. In another view, rows of shark teeth are shown, with a replacement tooth moving up.

pages.text: Most sharks are fish eaters Many of the largest sharks eat sea lions, dolphins, and other sharks These large sharks have triangular teeth with edges as sharp as knives The teeth help the shark catch and hold onto its prey The sharp teeth also help the shark tear its prey into chunks that it can swallow Other sharks, such as catsharks, eat clams, crabs, and lobsters These sharks have flat teeth for crushing and grinding shells The huge whale shark has tiny teeth but doesn’t use them when eating It swallows very small ocean plants and animals, called plankton, that float on or near the ocean’s surface It swims with its enormous mouth open Special filters in its gills catch the plankton and let the water flow through.
pages.brief: A large shark with sharp triangular teeth catches a sea lion. A catshark uses flat teeth to crush clams, crabs, and lobsters. A huge whale shark swims with its enormous mouth open, filtering tiny plankton from the ocean surface.

pages.text: Do You Know? Reproduction Most kinds of sharks bear live young Baby sharks are called pups Few pups survive to become adult sharks A few kinds of sharks, including the dogfish, lay eggs that hatch a few months later Each egg is protected by a leathery egg case The cases are rectangular, and many have string-shaped ends that attach to seaweed Some people call shark egg cases “mermaids’ purses ” Shark Attacks Many people are afraid of sharks, but most sharks do not attack humans In fact, bees kill more people each year than sharks do Only a few kinds of sharks are known to attack humans regularly One of these is the great white shark Great white sharks usually eat large animals, such as sea lions and other sharks Do You Know?
pages.brief: Baby sharks called pups swim near an adult, showing live young. A dogfish egg case, rectangular with string-like ends, attaches to seaweed. A great white shark swims near sea lions and other sharks in the ocean.

pages.text: Even small sharks may bite if disturbed or surprised Shark attacks are usually the result of people swimming in shark territory Sharks also confuse humans with their prey Many shark attacks involve the shark taking one “test bite” and then swimming away when it realizes that the human is not its prey Strange Sharks One of the strangest looking sharks is the hammerhead shark It has a flat head with a large lobe on each side The eyes and nostrils are positioned on the ends of these lobes Its strange head shape helps the hammerhead see around and behind it.
pages.brief: A small shark opens its mouth near a person swimming in shark territory, then swims away after a test bite. Nearby, a hammerhead shark has a flat head with eyes and nostrils on the ends of its lobes.

pages.text: Shark Survival People hunt sharks for many reasons Sharkskin is used to make shoes, belts, and wallets Shark oil is used in many cosmetics Shark teeth are used for jewelry Many people eat shark meat Chefs use shark fins to make a popular soup, and the sharks usually die when their fins are removed Many kinds of sharks are now in danger of extinction (being completely wiped out) People often do not protest when sharks are killed because sharks are thought to be mean and dangerous However, most sharks are not dangerous to humans.
pages.brief: People hunt sharks. Shoes, belts, and wallets are made from sharkskin; cosmetics contain shark oil; jewelry is made from shark teeth; shark meat is eaten; shark fins go into soup. A shark swims in the ocean, now in danger of extinction.

pages.text: Sharks do not reproduce nearly as quickly as other fish When they are killed, it takes much longer for their numbers to increase again Sharks are an important part of the balance of life in the world’s oceans They have as much right to exist as any other animal plankton (n.) page 12 tiny plants and animals that live on or near the ocean’s surface extinction (n.) page 18 the process by which an entire group of animals or plants dies out dorsal fin (n.) page 9 a fin on the back of fish and some marine mammals cartilage (n.) page 5 an elastic tissue that makes up the skeletons of sharks, rays, and skates camouflage (adj.) page 8 relating to a pattern that helps something blend in with its surroundings Glossary.
pages.brief: Sharks swim in the world's oceans, an important part of the balance of life. Compared with other fish, sharks reproduce slowly, so their numbers take much longer to increase when they are killed. Plankton floats on or near the ocean's surface.

books.title: Fireworks
books.art_why: The book includes fireworks history from ancient China, where real photographs are impossible, so drawings fit the historical scenes.

pages.text: Introduction The celebration began on a tiny island in the Pacific Ocean. Then, as Earth turned, midnight arrived in Sydney, Australia. Rings of fire exploded over the city’s famous opera house. Firecrackers popped in Hong Kong. Skyrockets flew over Bombay, the Egyptian pyramids, and Moscow. The Eiffel Tower shot bright sparks from its top like foam from a champagne bottle. Mexico City and Chicago were lit red, gold, and green. All around the world, fireworks welcomed the new year.
pages.brief: A nighttime view of Earth turning from a tiny Pacific island toward Sydney, where rings of fire explode above the Opera House. In other city scenes, firecrackers pop in Hong Kong, skyrockets fly over Bombay, the Egyptian pyramids, and Moscow, sparks shoot from the Eiffel Tower, and red, gold, and green fireworks light Mexico City and Chicago.

pages.text: Fireworks combine science and art to create some of the most beautiful displays ever seen. The making and launching of fireworks is called pyrotechnics (PIE-roe-TECK-nicks). In most cases, this dangerous craft is still performed by hand. Families pass down secret fireworks-making skills and formulas from generation to generation.
pages.brief: In a family workshop, adults show younger family members how fireworks are made by hand. They stand together around a work area with ingredients and firework parts, passing down secret formulas and skills from one generation to the next. The scene feels careful and close, showing a dangerous craft kept within a family.

pages.text: History of Fireworks No one is sure when fireworks first shot into the sky. But we do know that it happened in China over 1,000 years ago. Legend says that a Chinese cook accidentally created gunpowder by mixing ingredients in his kitchen.
pages.brief: In an ancient Chinese kitchen, a cook mixes ingredients and accidentally creates black gunpowder. He looks surprised as a small burst of fire and smoke rises from the mixture. The simple kitchen scene suggests the legendary moment over one thousand years ago when fireworks were first made, with no exact date known.

pages.text: Chinese people packed this explosive black powder into bamboo or paper tubes. The powder shot fire out of the tubes, much like Roman candles do today. Someone discovered that if a wooden carving was placed on top of the gunpowder, the carving would shoot into the sky. One carving of a dragon even had gunpowder in its mouth. The dragon seemed to spray fire as it flew.
pages.brief: Chinese fireworks makers pack black powder into bamboo and paper tubes, and fire shoots out of the open ends. Above one tube, a wooden dragon carving is placed on top of gunpowder; with powder in its mouth, the dragon seems to spray fire as it flies into the sky.

pages.text: The secret of gunpowder passed to countries in the Middle East and then on to Europe. But it was mostly used in weapons to fire cannons and guns. Often, armies shot their cannons to celebrate a victory. Different countries began mixing certain chemicals with the gunpowder to create brighter flashes, louder bangs, and color. The Italians soon became famous for their colorful displays. The Grucci family, now living in the United States, continues the Italian tradition of fireworks mastery.
pages.brief: The secret of gunpowder travels from China to the Middle East and Europe, where soldiers fire cannons and guns. Armies shoot cannons in victory celebrations while fireworks makers mix chemicals into gunpowder for brighter flashes, louder bangs, and color. Italian displays become famous, and the Grucci family in the United States continues that tradition.

pages.text: How Fireworks Are Made All fireworks start with gunpowder. To create colors, fireworks makers combine special chemicals with the gunpowder. These chemicals burn with different-colored flames. Surprisingly, most of these chemicals are kinds of salt. They may also mix flakes of metal with the gunpowder. When the powder explodes, these flakes become glowing hot, creating a shower of sparks.
pages.brief: Fireworks makers begin with gunpowder and add special chemicals and metal flakes. The chemicals are kinds of salt, and when the powder explodes, the hot metal flakes glow and create a shower of bright sparks. The scene focuses on the ingredients and the glowing sparks that make fireworks colorful.

pages.text: Different chemicals burn with different colors. Copper, the metal in pennies, burns blue-green. The same color change happens, only much more slowly, to pennies when they turn green. This is why the Statue of Liberty, which is made of copper, looks green. The chart below lists some other chemicals and the colors they produce. Fireworks Chemicals Chemical Effect Copper salts Blue Strontium salts Red Sodium Yellow Barium nitrate Green Potassium perchlorate Makes loud booms.
pages.brief: Copper burns blue-green, and the same slow color change appears on old pennies and on the Statue of Liberty, which is made of copper and looks green. Nearby, different chemical salts burn in blue, red, yellow, and green flames, showing how fireworks makers choose colors for their displays.

pages.text: Fireworks cause sound because the intense heat expands the air around the firework. The air is pushed outward in a wave. Your ear picks up this wave as a loud sound. Sometimes your chest and feet can also feel the wave vibrating. This is the same way that lightning creates thunder. The whistles come from the hot gasses combustion creates. Fireworks makers put tiny paper whistles inside the shells. When the stars combust, the hot gasses “blow” the whistles, creating the sound.
pages.brief: A bursting firework sends out a wave of expanding air, and a nearby person feels the loud boom in their ears, chest, and feet, like thunder after lightning. Inside the shell, hot gases from burning stars blow tiny paper whistles, creating the whistling sounds that come from the firework.

pages.text: Fireworks makers roll the colored or sparkling gunpowder into small balls called stars. Some stars are a single color, while others are layered with different colors. They pack the stars inside stiff paper shells. Hundreds of stars can fit in one shell. If the fireworks maker packs the stars in a globe shape, the firework will explode in a globe of fire. If he or she packs it in a star shape, it will explode into a star. If he or she packs it in a smiley-face shape, it will explode into a smiley face. Parts of a Firework.
pages.brief: Fireworks makers roll colored and sparkling gunpowder into small balls called stars. They pack hundreds of stars into stiff paper shells in different arrangements. A shell packed in a globe shape explodes as a globe of fire, one packed in a star shape bursts into a star, and one packed in a smiley-face shape bursts into a smiley face.

pages.text: Sometimes each star has its own paper tube. The tubes force the stars to shoot away from the main firework in streaks of light. And sometimes the shell is packed solid with powder that creates a single flash and a huge bang, called a salute. At the center of every shape is a ball of gunpowder called a bursting charge. The bursting charge explodes like a firecracker. It lights the stars and sends them out into the sky.
pages.brief: Some stars sit inside paper tubes so they shoot away from the main firework in streaks of light. Other shells are packed solid with powder to make a single flash and huge bang called a salute. At the center of every shape a ball of gunpowder called the bursting charge explodes like a firecracker and sends stars into the sky.

pages.text: The last part of the shell is the lift charge. This is a container of powder that will shoot the entire shell high into the sky. Usually, the lift charge is ordinary gunpowder. But sometimes it creates a streak of color as the firework rises.
pages.brief: At the bottom of a firework shell, a container of powder called the lift charge waits to shoot the whole shell high into the sky. Usually it holds ordinary gunpowder, but sometimes the lift charge creates a bright streak of color as the firework rises upward.

pages.text: Do You Know? Combustion is the scientific term for burning or exploding. Almost all combustion requires oxygen. A flame under a glass dome will soon go out when it uses up all the oxygen. Gunpowder has oxygen right in it, which makes it extra flammable. Combustion also makes the air around it expand, or grow larger. When gunpowder combusts inside a shell, the air inside the shell expands, forcing the shell to burst open. 3 the heat produces 4 the shell bursts.
pages.brief: A flame burns under a glass dome and soon goes out after using up the oxygen. Nearby, gunpowder inside a firework shell combusts; the heat makes the air inside expand until the shell bursts open. Because gunpowder carries oxygen within it, it is extra flammable and can burn or explode even without outside air.

pages.text: Each firework has a special series of fuses that control when the firework explodes. The first fuse, called a leader, lights the lift charge, sending the firework flying. The lift charge then lights a time fuse. The material of the time fuse burns at a steady rate. The fireworks makers know just how long to cut the fuse so it burns until the shell is at the right height. The time fuse then sets off the bursting charge. Sometimes a shell will have smaller shells inside it. In that case, the bursting charge lights more time fuses. These will set off the smaller shells once they’re the right distance away from the main shell. Loading shells with black powder.
pages.brief: A firework shell shows its series of fuses. The leader lights the lift charge and sends the shell flying then the lift charge lights a time fuse that burns at a steady rate. When the time fuse reaches the bursting charge it sets off the shell and inside some shells more time fuses light smaller shells at the right distance.

pages.text: Creating the Show It can take up to two days to set up a twenty-minute fireworks show. First, everything must be designed on a diagram. Each shell will be fired in a specific order, and everything must be set up so that each one goes in turn. Workers begin by building batteries, or wooden racks. If the show is near water, the batteries are put on a boat, safely away from the crowd. Some batteries sit on the sides of buildings, such as the Washington Monument or the Eiffel Tower. Each battery holds a group of metal tubes called mortars. Each mortar holds one shell. It shoots the shell the way a cannon shoots a cannonball. All the mortars are numbered according to the diagram.
