pages.brief: Workers build wooden racks called batteries and place groups of metal tubes called mortars inside them. Each mortar holds one shell, ready to shoot like a cannon. Near water, a battery sits on a boat away from the crowd; other batteries line the sides of buildings such as the Washington Monument or the Eiffel Tower.

pages.text: The finished shells are also numbered. When they arrive on the site, they are carefully placed in the correct mortars. Workers connect the shells’ leaders, or main fuses, to electrical matches. And each electric match is connected to the firing panel, which is the control panel for the whole show. In the past, the fireworks maker had to push buttons on the panel to get each match to light. He or she had to pay close attention in order to avoid mistakes. Today, most firing panels are computerized.
pages.brief: Numbered shells arrive at the site and are placed carefully into the correct numbered mortars. Workers connect each shell’s leader to an electrical match and each match runs to the firing panel that controls the whole show. In the past a fireworks maker pushed buttons by hand today most firing panels are computerized.

pages.text: Everyone checks the fuse connections, the placement of the shells and mortars, and the firing order. Then they check them again. A mistake could set the fireworks off incorrectly, ruining the show and possibly even injuring people.
pages.brief: A crew checks the fuse connections, the placement of shells and mortars, and the firing order. They look closely at every part, then check everything again. Their careful movements show why they must be so precise: one mistake could set fireworks off incorrectly, ruin the show, and possibly injure people.

pages.text: On the night of the show, the crew puts on helmets, goggles, and fireproof clothing. This gear protects the workers from falling sparks, ash, and paper. The workers stay close by to make sure nothing goes wrong. But once the switch is flipped, the computer takes over and begins lighting matches. The show explodes in a shower of color and sound.
pages.brief: On the night of the show, the crew wears helmets, goggles, and fireproof clothing to protect against falling sparks, ash, and paper. They stay close by as one worker flips the switch. Then the computer takes over, lighting matches in order, and the show explodes into a shower of color and sound.

pages.text: Computer firing panels have become so precise that fireworks can be set to music. A designer chooses a favorite piece of music. The designer listens to the music over and over, imagining where to put a purple fountain, a golden blast, or flashes and crashes. The firing panel is programmed to light the shells in time with the music.
pages.brief: A designer listens to a favorite piece of music over and over, imagining where a purple fountain, a golden blast, or flashes and crashes should appear in the sky. The computer firing panel is then programmed to light each shell in time with the music making fireworks dance to the beat.

pages.text: Fireworks Safety Fireworks explode, and explosions can be deadly. Fireworks injure about 10,000 people every year in the United States alone. Firecrackers can blow off a hand. Sparklers can send a glowing-hot spark of metal into someone’s eye. And illegally stored fireworks can cause devastating fires. In addition, fireworks cause smoke and noise, and they often terrify animals and alarm people. Many states have laws against using fireworks. Those laws exist to protect people. Using, storing, or selling illegal fireworks can lead to arrest, fines, or even jail. It is best to leave fireworks to the trained professionals.
pages.brief: A firecracker explodes near a hand, a sparkler sends a glowing-hot spark toward an eye, and illegally stored fireworks start a dangerous fire. Smoke and noise frighten animals and alarm people. Because laws in many states protect people, illegal use, storage, or sale can lead to arrest, fines, or jail, so trained professionals should handle fireworks.

pages.text: If you do watch fireworks, be sure to follow these safety tips: • Always watch from a safe distance, and never approach the fireworks. • Never pick up debris from fireworks. It may still contain explosive gunpowder. • Bring ear protection. Long exposure to loud noises can damage your hearing. • Never, ever light fireworks yourself. If consumer fireworks are legal in your state, always have an adult light them. • Have water handy to put out any fires or sparks.
pages.brief: People watch fireworks from a safe distance and never approach them. A fallen piece of firework debris lies on the ground and a person keeps away from it because it may still contain explosive gunpowder. Someone wears ear protection against loud noises an adult lights legal consumer fireworks and a bucket of water sits nearby.

books.title: Amelia Earhart: A Legend in Flight
books.art_why: A book about a named famous person, Amelia Earhart, so cartoon artwork fits the series rule.

pages.text: Amelia Earhart: A Legend in Flight.
pages.brief: Cover portrait of Amelia Earhart as a young aviator: short tousled hair, leather flight jacket, goggles pushed up on her forehead, standing calmly with a small 1930s airplane parked behind her under an open sky.

pages.text: Introduction The airplane bounced among the clouds. Giant black storm clouds lay ahead. The year was 1932. The airplane carried Amelia Earhart. She had been the first woman to ride in an airplane over the Atlantic Ocean. Now, if she made it, she would be the first woman to fly an airplane over the Atlantic. And she would be the first person to have crossed the Atlantic in an airplane twice. But first she had to succeed, and the trip was dangerous. Airplanes in the 1930s were small, and they didn’t have the instruments that today’s pilots do. A pilot had to go by her sense of sight, keeping tight control of the airplane.
pages.brief: A small 1930s airplane bounces among white clouds, giant black storm clouds looming ahead. Inside the cockpit, Amelia Earhart sits alert, hands on the controls, flying by sight because the little plane has no modern instruments.

pages.text: The black clouds ahead were too large to fly around, so Amelia pointed the little plane right into them. Ice froze the plane’s controls, sending it into a tailspin. Amelia struggled to get control. Finally, the ice melted and Amelia was able to pull the plane out of its spin. Many hours later, Amelia set the plane down in Northern Ireland. She had crossed the Atlantic Ocean in an airplane she flew herself. She had already been famous. Now, she would be a legend. But Amelia Earhart would be most remembered for something else. While trying to fly around the world, she disappeared.
pages.brief: The little plane plunges into the black clouds and ice coats its controls, sending it spinning in a tailspin while Amelia fights to pull it out. Later the same plane sits safely on the ground in green Northern Ireland countryside.

pages.text: Winged Machines The world’s first airplane flight happened in 1903. Two brothers, Wilbur and Orville Wright, successfully flew their winged machine in North Carolina. Many people thought the idea of flying was exciting. It was also dangerous. Planes were fragile and slow. They did not fly well in bad weather, and many pilots died in crashes. By 1937, airplanes had improved a lot. Engineers designed better airplanes, but accidents still happened.
pages.brief: Wilbur and Orville Wright launch their fragile winged machine over the sand at North Carolina in 1903. Nearby, engineers sketch and build improved airplanes, while slow, flimsy early planes struggle in bad weather.

pages.text: Kansas Youth Anyone who knew Amelia as a child could hardly have been surprised by her later accomplishments. She was born in Kansas in 1897. She spent most of her time with her family and friends. They climbed around the banks of the Missouri River. Amelia made up games for the children to play. She and her sister were such active children that their mother made “ bloomers ” for them to wear. Unlike dresses, bloomers allowed the girls to be as active as the boys. When Amelia was twenty-one, her family moved to California. One day she attended an air show. The airplanes dazzled her, flying in loops and doing stunts. She knew then that she wanted to fly. With her parents’ help, Amelia took piloting lessons and saved enough money to buy an airplane. Before long, she was flying in air shows herself.
pages.brief: Young Amelia climbs the banks of the Missouri River in Kansas with her sister and friends, wearing loose bloomers instead of dresses. Years later, now twenty-one in California, she watches dazzled as airplanes loop and stunt above an air show crowd.

pages.text: Time to Fly Amelia later moved to Boston and found a job at Denison House. It was a place where people who were poor, especially children, could receive help. She loved her work there, but then the chance of a lifetime presented itself. George Putnam, a publicist, searched for a woman to be the first to ride in an airplane over the Atlantic. It was a dangerous idea. Three women had died trying to cross the Atlantic the year before.
pages.brief: Amelia works at Denison House in Boston, surrounded by poor children she helps and teaches. Across the city, publicist George Putnam searches for a woman brave enough to ride an airplane across the Atlantic Ocean.

pages.text: Only men had ever crossed the Atlantic in an airplane. Anyone who would try it had to withstand danger and fatigue. George thought Amelia Earhart was perfect, and she was eager to go. • Magazine editor • Writer • Airline executive • Professor She also helped start the “Ninety-Nines,” a group of women pilots that still exists today.
pages.brief: George Putnam presents Amelia with the dangerous Atlantic chance, and she agrees eagerly. Beside her are the roles she takes on — magazine editor, writer, airline executive, professor — and a gathering of women pilots she helped organise.

pages.text: Amelia was just a passenger on that 1928 flight, but her life would never be the same. The first woman to cross the Atlantic made headlines around the world. After the flight, she was famous and busy writing books and giving speeches about flying. She also designed clothing and luggage for active women like herself and even helped launch two airlines. Later, she married George Putnam. She also continued to fly.
pages.brief: Amelia rides as a passenger on the 1928 Atlantic flight, then steps out into worldwide fame: writing books, giving speeches, sketching clothing and luggage for active women, helping launch two airlines, and marrying George Putnam.

pages.text: By the time she was thirty-nine years old, Amelia had made every major flight there was, except for one. The greatest challenge left was to fly around the world. Only one pilot had ever flown around the world. But he didn’t follow the equator, the longest and most difficult route. This was the route Amelia would fly. Would she make it? By this time, no one doubted Amelia Earhart’s flying skill. On May 21, 1937, she took off with her navigator, Fred Noonan. They went from California to Florida in a Lockheed Electra.
pages.brief: Amelia, thirty-nine, stands before a map planning the longest route around the world along the equator. On May 21, 1937, she lifts off in a Lockheed Electra with navigator Fred Noonan, flying from California to Florida.

pages.text: ASIA ASIA AFRICA AFRICA SOUTH SOUTH AMERICA AMERICA Last Flight Amelia and Fred first stopped the Electra in Florida. The new plane had crossed the entire North American continent. Next, they flew to South America, Africa, India, Asia, and Australia. It appeared that Amelia Earhart would once again pull off a historic flight without a hitch. On June 29, 1937, they stopped in New Guinea, just north of Australia. There, they fueled the airplane and checked their maps. When they took off again, there was no hint of any trouble to come.
pages.brief: The silver Lockheed Electra crosses South America, Africa, India, Asia and Australia. On June 29, 1937, it rests at New Guinea, north of Australia, where Amelia and Fred fuel the plane and check their maps before taking off again.

pages.text: ASIA ASIA India India Hawaii Lae Howland Island AUSTRALIA AUSTRALIA As they flew close to Howland Island, their radio messages became odd. The U.S. Coast Guard cutter Itasca waited offshore to receive their signals and help them find the island. Those radio signals were irregular and strange. Amelia spoke of a storm, yet the weather over the island was clear. More than twenty hours into the flight, Amelia’s voice said, “We’re running north and south.” She was never heard from again.
pages.brief: The U.S. Coast Guard cutter Itasca waits offshore near Howland Island under clear skies, listening for signals. In the Electra, Amelia and Fred send strange, irregular radio messages as they search for the tiny island below.

pages.text: What Happened to Amelia? This question is still a mystery today. The Itasca and the U.S. Navy began searching for Amelia’s plane. The search continued for weeks. No sign of the plane, Amelia, or Fred was found. After a year of searching, Amelia’s husband believed that she died at sea. But is that the full story? Some people think Amelia and Fred survived an emergency landing and were picked up by a Japanese ship.
pages.brief: The Itasca and U.S. Navy ships search the empty ocean for weeks, finding no trace of the plane, Amelia or Fred. Amelia's husband concludes she died at sea, while others imagine a Japanese ship picking the pair up.

pages.text: Others think that Amelia landed the plane, but at a different island. There, she and Fred were able to live on native foods but died of either sickness or old age. Many people believe the easiest answer is that the plane landed in the water. Perhaps Amelia and Fred drowned before they inflated their life raft. Whatever happened, there is no doubt that Amelia Earhart is one of the greatest Americans of the 20th century. She showed everyone that women didn’t have to live with limits. She showed people that anyone could fly. She was a legend.
pages.brief: Other theories show Amelia landing on a different island, living on native foods with Fred, or the plane settling into the water beside an unopened life raft. Her story closes as a legend who showed women had no limits.

books.title: Queen Elizabeth I
books.art_why: Named famous person: Queen Elizabeth I.

pages.text: Queen Elizabeth l.
pages.brief: A cartoon portrait of Queen Elizabeth I, shown from the waist up in a rich royal gown, with a crown and calm, steady expression. She stands in a plain palace hall, looking ahead as a powerful English queen.

pages.text: Elizabeth’s Family Many people think Elizabeth Tudor was the greatest English ruler of all time. She came from a powerful family. Before Elizabeth was born, her father, King Henry VIII of England, fell in love with Anne Boleyn while he was still married to his first wife. Henry wanted to end his marriage and marry Anne. This was not allowed in the Catholic Church at the time. Against the wishes of the Catholic Church, Henry started another church and ended his marriage. This church became known as the Church of England.
pages.brief: King Henry VIII stands with Anne Boleyn in a grand English court while his first wife sits apart. Henry turns away from Catholic Church leaders, who frown. He points toward a new church building, showing his break from Rome and the start of the Church of England.

pages.text: Henry was free of the Catholic Church. He married Anne Boleyn. Anne gave birth to Elizabeth Tudor on September 7, 1533. Anne was worried after she gave birth to Elizabeth. She thought that Henry might be unhappy with her for not giving him a son. She was right. Henry already had a daughter, Mary, with his first wife. He wanted a son to take over as king when he died. In time, Henry ended their marriage and had her put to death. Elizabeth was only three years old when her mother died.
pages.brief: Anne Boleyn cradles newborn Elizabeth in a Tudor chamber, her face worried. King Henry VIII stands nearby looking displeased, while a nurse holds his older daughter Mary. In a shadowed corner, Anne is led away, and three-year-old Elizabeth stands alone with a sad expression.

pages.text: Prince Edward In 1537, Henry married his third wife, Jane, who gave birth to Prince Edward. At last, Henry had the son he always wanted. Jane, however, died a few days after Edward was born. Henry’s sixth and last wife was Catherine Parr. She told Henry to decide who would one day take over his throne, and finally he did. Prince Edward would be first in line, Mary would be second, and Elizabeth would be third. When Henry VIII died in 1547, nine-year-old Prince Edward became king. His rule as king was short. Edward died when he was only fifteen years old. Elizabeth’s older sister Mary became queen.
pages.brief: Jane gives birth to Prince Edward in a royal bedchamber, then lies weak as servants grieve. Young Edward later sits on a throne with a crown, while King Henry VIII and Catherine Parr stand nearby. Queen Mary appears in the background, ready to rule after Edward.

pages.text: Mary and Elizabeth Mary had been raised in the Catholic religion. In her time, some people began a new Protestant religion. Mary’s goal as queen was to end the Protestant religion and make the Catholic religion England’s main religion again. Mary did not like people who did not follow the Catholic teachings. She was known for her strict punishments and often ordered Protestants to be put to death. This earned her the nickname “Bloody Mary.” Elizabeth, on the other hand, was Protestant. The faith was important to her, but Elizabeth attended Catholic church to please Mary. Mary didn’t trust Elizabeth and believed she was practicing the Protestant faith in secret. When some people plotted to remove Mary as queen, she was sure that Elizabeth was behind it. Mary had Elizabeth arrested and put in jail for two months. When Elizabeth was let go, she remained under Mary’s watch for a year.
pages.brief: Queen Mary, stern in Catholic royal robes, stands in a chapel while Elizabeth kneels at a Catholic service and glances sideways. Protestant prisoners wait in shadow. Elizabeth is later shown inside a small jail cell, watched by guards, then kept under Mary’s watchful eye.

pages.text: Queen Elizabeth In 1558, Mary became ill and died. Elizabeth, who was next in line to the throne, was crowned queen on January 15, 1559. Elizabeth announced to the world that she was a Protestant. However, Elizabeth had an open mind. She worked with both Catholics and Protestants and tried to make peace. She was not always successful. Protestants thought she was too easy on Catholics, and some Catholics felt she turned her back on them.
pages.brief: Elizabeth is crowned queen in a grand abbey, wearing a crown and holding royal symbols. Catholic and Protestant advisers stand on either side, some frowning and some hopeful. Elizabeth looks calm, with open hands, trying to keep peace between the two groups.

pages.text: From the beginning of Elizabeth’s time as queen, English leaders tried to find a husband for her. If Elizabeth married and had a child, England would have a future king or queen. Elizabeth received many offers to marry but did not accept any. Elizabeth’s Fashion Elizabeth had fair skin and hair, features considered beautiful in Tudor England. As a young girl, Elizabeth dressed modestly, but as queen, she preferred to wear gowns of bright reds and oranges. Her robes were often decorated with rich pearls and jewels. Such elaborate clothing gave a sense of absolute royal power and authority.
pages.brief: Elizabeth stands in a bright red and orange gown decorated with pearls and jewels, her fair hair and skin shown clearly. Around her, advisers present marriage offers, but she holds up a hand and turns away. In a small memory, young Elizabeth wears a simple modest dress.

pages.text: Battles Elizabeth faced many challenges, but one of her biggest problems came from Mary, Queen of Scots. Mary, Elizabeth’s cousin, was the Catholic queen of Scotland. Many Catholics didn’t think Elizabeth should be queen. Different Catholic groups plotted to remove Elizabeth so Mary could be the English queen. They wanted England to be a Catholic country. In 1586, Elizabeth learned that there was a plot to kill her. Mary was involved. Elizabeth had her put to death. Mary died on February 8, 1587. Her death angered Catholics everywhere. King Philip II of Spain, a Catholic, was one of them. Philip thought that Queen Elizabeth had gone too far and should be removed as queen. He also wanted England to be a Catholic country again.
pages.brief: Mary, Queen of Scots stands in a Scottish court with Catholic supporters plotting around a table. Elizabeth receives news of a murder plot and signs an order. Later, Mary is shown condemned. King Philip II of Spain frowns angrily in his palace, planning to remove Elizabeth.

pages.text: In 1588, Philip ordered a large group of ships to set sail and invade England. The ships were loaded with soldiers. Spain, however, was not prepared for the strength of the English. English ships forced the Spanish ships far to the north. Many Spanish ships crashed on the rocky shores, and many men died. Route of the Spanish, 1588.
pages.brief: A huge Spanish fleet sails toward England, crowded with soldiers. English ships attack and push the Spanish ships north. Stormy waves crash several Spanish ships against rocky northern shores, with sailors struggling in the sea. The scene shows the failed invasion and the route of the Spanish fleet.

pages.text: Elizabeth’s Successes Over time, Elizabeth reduced the religious fighting that had torn apart her country. The Protestant church became the official religion of England. There was great growth in education and the arts. More people than ever before learned to read and write. Theater became very popular during Elizabeth’s time and writers often brought plays and actors to her court. Some plays were about the events happening in England at the time, and some were comedies that Elizabeth enjoyed. She also loved poetry and playing music.
pages.brief: Elizabeth sits in a lively court theater, smiling at actors performing a comedy. Around her, writers hold plays and poetry, and children read books at a small school desk. Musicians play nearby, and Protestant and Catholic advisers stand more peacefully together.

pages.text: During her time as queen, Elizabeth developed a strong government and a powerful navy. Wanting to bring good things to the country she loved, she encouraged exploration of new places and trade with foreign countries. Trade of goods such as silk and food made money for England. England was set to become a global empire and the Elizabethan Age came to be known as the “Golden Age” in English history. As a result of growth during this time, England became one of the most important countries in the world.
pages.brief: Elizabeth looks over a busy harbor where English ships unload silk and food from distant lands. Explorers study maps, sailors load goods, and a strong navy patrols the sea. In the background, English towns and schools grow prosperous, showing the country becoming important.

pages.text: A Strong Leader Elizabeth died in 1603 at the age of sixty- nine. She ruled England for forty-four years. She named Protestant James VI, the son of Mary, Queen of Scots, as the new king. By doing so, she united Scotland and England. Elizabeth I was a well-educated, strong queen. She proved that a woman could be a successful ruler. At the same time, she earned the love and respect of her people.
pages.brief: An older Queen Elizabeth sits on her throne with a calm, proud expression, while courtiers bow and children wave. James VI of Scotland stands beside her as her chosen heir. Behind them, a map suggests England and Scotland united, and books show her education.

pages.text: Queen Elizabeth I 1533: Elizabeth born to Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn 1536: Anne Boleyn executed 1544: Henry orders his son and daughters as future leaders 1547: Henry VIII dies; Edward becomes king 1553: King Edward VI dies on July 6 1553: Mary crowned queen on October 1 1554: Mary orders Elizabeth jailed 1558: Mary dies; Elizabeth becomes queen 1587: Mary, Queen of Scots dies 1588: Elizabeth wins the fight against the Spanish 1603: Elizabeth dies on March 24; James I becomes king of England and Scotland, bringing the two countries together 1590: The arts begin to grow due to the support of Elizabeth.
pages.brief: A sequence of small cartoon scenes shows Elizabeth’s life: she is born to Henry VIII and Anne Boleyn, her mother is taken away, young Edward rules, Mary is crowned, Elizabeth is jailed, then crowned queen, Mary Queen of Scots dies, Spanish ships are defeated, the arts grow, and older Elizabeth names James king.

books.title: Jackie Robinson
books.art_why: The book is about a named famous person, Jackie Robinson.

pages.text: Introduction African Americans play a big part in professional sports today. For many years, however, black athletes weren’t allowed to play with white athletes. Jackie Robinson helped change all that.
pages.brief: A group of African American athletes playing professional sports today, with Jackie Robinson shown as a historical figure who helped bring about that change. Behind them, a simple scene suggests earlier years when black athletes were kept from playing alongside white athletes.

pages.text: The Early Years Jack Roosevelt Robinson was born into a poor Georgia family in 1919.
pages.brief: A poor African American family in Georgia in 1919, with baby Jack Roosevelt Robinson among them. The family is shown in a humble home setting, and the baby is the focus as the future Jackie Robinson.

pages.text: In college, he was a star on his school’s football, track, basketball, and baseball teams. His family had little money, however. He left college in 1941 to help support his family. He did not finish college.
pages.brief: Young Jackie Robinson in college, starring on his school’s football, track, basketball, and baseball teams. He is shown active in several sports, while his family’s lack of money is suggested by his leaving college in 1941 to help support them.

pages.text: Taking a Stand In December 1941, the United States entered a war. Like many young men, Robinson had to serve in the war. One day, he and a group of soldiers got on an army bus. The bus was segregated. White soldiers sat in the front and black soldiers in the back. Yet Robinson knew he was as good a soldier as the white men. He would not move to the back when he was told to. Robinson was arrested, but he had only stood up for what was right. He was let go.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson in army uniform during wartime, boarding a segregated army bus with a group of soldiers. White soldiers sit in the front and black soldiers in the back. Robinson stands firm, refusing to move to the back, and is later arrested and let go.

pages.text: You’re Hired! After his time in the army, Robinson played baseball. In 1945, however, baseball was segregated, too. White and black athletes played in different leagues.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson playing baseball after his army service, with white and black athletes shown in separate leagues in 1945. The scene shows that baseball was segregated, with Robinson among the black players in a different league from white players.

pages.text: Robinson felt that there should not be different baseball leagues based on skin color. So did Branch Rickey. He ran the Brooklyn Dodgers. Rickey wanted the Dodgers to be the first white team with a black player. Rickey knew that this player would not only have to be great at baseball. He would also have to face prejudice because he was African American.
pages.brief: Branch Rickey, who runs the Brooklyn Dodgers, with Jackie Robinson. Rickey wants the Dodgers to be the first white team with a black player, and he knows the player must be great at baseball and face prejudice as an African American.

pages.text: Rickey hired Robinson. He had one condition, though. Robinson could only fight prejudice one way—by playing great baseball. A Team of Two A Team of Two.
pages.brief: Branch Rickey hiring Jackie Robinson, with one condition: Robinson can only fight prejudice by playing great baseball. The two are shown together as a team of two, with Rickey making the agreement and Robinson accepting the challenge.

pages.text: Number 42 Takes the Field Wearing number 42, Robinson took the field on April 15, 1947. A crowd of twenty-six thousand people watched as he walked to the plate. Insults rang out from the other team’s dugout. Robinson just played ball.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson wearing number 42 taking the field on April 15, 1947, as twenty-six thousand people watch him walk to the plate. Insults ring out from the other team’s dugout, but Robinson just plays ball.

pages.text: Equal rights won that day. So did the Dodgers. As for Robinson, he went on to have a great career. Another Great Steal Another Great Steal.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson on the field as equal rights win that day and the Dodgers also win. He is shown in the middle of a great baseball career, with another great steal adding to the moment.

pages.text: In 1962, he became the first African American to get into the Baseball Hall of Fame.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson in 1962 as the first African American inducted into the Baseball Hall of Fame. He is shown honored for his career, standing among baseball greats as the first African American to receive that recognition.

pages.text: His Number, His Day His Number, His Day.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson’s number 42 is honored, and a special day celebrates him. He is shown as a baseball figure whose number and day keep his memory alive, with people remembering his place in the sport.

pages.text: Beyond Baseball Robinson stopped playing baseball in 1957. Then he went into business. He also continued to work for equal rights for all people. He died in 1972. Today in the United States, more people of color play in the world of sports than ever before. We all have Number 42 to thank for that.
pages.brief: Jackie Robinson after he stopped playing baseball in 1957, going into business and continuing to work for equal rights for all people. He is shown later in life, and today more people of color play in sports because of Number 42.

books.title: Slithery Snakes
books.art_why: Snakes are real animals that exist today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction Snakes are reptiles, a class of animals that also includes lizards and turtles. Snakes have no limbs. They come in many lengths, patterns, and colors. There are several thousand types of snakes. They live in oceans, in trees, and on land, and they have adapted to survive in unusual ways.
pages.brief: A group of snakes with many lengths, patterns, and colors appears in three settings: one swimming in ocean water, one coiled in a tree, and one moving on land. Their bodies show different shapes and unusual adaptations.

pages.text: Where Snakes Live Snakes live almost everywhere except Antarctica. Some places don’t have any snakes. Snakes do not live in the wild on islands such as Ireland, New Zealand, and Iceland. Some snakes in the wild may live up to twenty-five years. Biggest and Smallest The largest snake is the green anaconda. A full-grown green anaconda can be close to 10 meters (33 ft.) long and weigh more than 230 kilograms (507 lb.). One of the smallest snakes is the thread snake. It is only about 12 centimeters (4 in.) long.
pages.brief: A green anaconda stretches close to 10 meters long and weighs more than 230 kilograms, while a tiny thread snake only about 12 centimeters long is shown nearby. Their surroundings suggest places where snakes live and other places where they do not live in the wild.

pages.text: Snake Traits Like all reptiles, snakes are cold-blooded. Their body temperature changes as the temperature around them changes. If a snake needs to warm up, it lies in the sun. If it needs to cool down, it rests in the shade. Snakes become much less active in winter. Some snakes that live through cold winters find a place underground or beneath a rock pile to stay warm. Another way snakes stay warm is by looping around each other to share body heat.
pages.brief: A snake lies stretched in bright sunlight to warm its cold-blooded body. Nearby another rests in shade to cool down. Underground and beneath a rock pile, snakes stay warm through cold winter, and two loop around each other to share body heat.

pages.text: Snakes have a long backbone with ribs. Their backbone is made up of many separate bones. Because of this, they can move in many different ways. A snake’s body is covered in scales. The scales protect it. They also help keep the snake dry. The scales grow from the snake’s skin. Some snakes’ scales are colorful. Other scales help them blend in with their surroundings. Since snakes have no arms or legs, they use their scales and muscles to move. The scales on their belly tightly grip the surface beneath them. Their muscles help them move from side to side, or slither, along the ground. Some snakes even use their muscles and scales to climb trees.
pages.brief: A snake's long backbone with many separate bones and ribs is visible inside its body. Outside, overlapping scales cover it. Without arms or legs, the snake uses belly scales and side-to-side muscles to slither along the ground; another climbs a tree.

pages.text: Snake scales look like a single sheet of skin. Snakes don’t really shed skin. Instead, they shed the outer layers of their scales. Snakes may shed up to four times per year. This is called molting. During molting, a snake rubs against a hard object such as a rock or log. Rubbing helps its skin stretch and split. Then the snake crawls out and leaves it behind. Snakes shed for several reasons. Young snakes shed more often than older snakes because they outgrow the skin faster. Unlike other animals, snakes’ skin does not stretch as they grow. Another reason snakes shed is to get rid of parasites that may grab on to their old skin.
pages.brief: A snake rubs its body against a hard rock beside a log. Its outer scale layers split and stretch, and the snake crawls forward out of the old covering, leaving it behind. The shed skin looks like a thin, single sheet nearby.

pages.text: Scales also protect a snake’s eyes. Unlike many animals, snakes do not have eyelids. Instead, each eye is covered with a clear scale that protects it from drying out. Because of this, snakes can’t blink. Snakes do not have ears you can see. Instead, sound passes through the jawbone to the inner ear, which sends a signal to the snake’s brain. Snakes have developed a different way to hear sounds with this method.
pages.brief: Close view of a snake's head: a clear scale covers each eye, and there are no eyelids, so it cannot blink. It has no visible ears; sound travels through its jawbone toward the inner ear. The snake rests with its head raised slightly.

pages.text: Another important feature of a snake is its tongue. A snake smells with its tongue. Its forked tongue picks up scents from the air. Scent particles stick to the tongue. The snake then pulls its tongue back into its mouth. When its tongue touches the roof of its mouth, a special organ helps to identify the scent. Some snakes are able to sense the heat of animals nearby. Pits near the snake’s eyes can sense the air temperature. This kind of sensing helps these snakes judge distances so they can hunt for prey in the dark.
pages.brief: A snake flicks out its forked tongue to pick up scent particles from the air, then pulls the tongue back toward the roof of its mouth. Pits near its eyes sense the warmth of nearby animals, helping it judge distance in darkness.

pages.text: Hunting and Eating Snakes are carnivores, or meat eaters. They eat other animals in one of three ways. Some snakes use venom when biting their prey. Other snakes, called constrictors, squeeze their prey to death before swallowing it. Some snakes grab their prey with their jaws and swallow it alive. Most snakes’ upper and lower jaws are loosely connected. As a result, a snake can spread its jaws and open its mouth wide enough to swallow large objects. Snakes’ teeth are mainly made for catching and holding prey. Their fangs and other teeth curve backward, which pushes food toward their throat. They push their breathing tube out of their mouth so they can breathe as they swallow their prey whole. Snakes use strong muscles to move the prey into the stomach and intestines. Strong stomach acids turn the prey into liquid so the snake can digest it easier.
pages.brief: A snake opens its loosely connected jaws wide around large prey. Its backward-curving teeth hold the food and push it toward the throat. It extends a breathing tube from its mouth while swallowing, and strong muscles move the prey inward.

pages.text: How Snakes Are Born Most snakes that live in cold areas mate in the late spring or early summer. Snakes that live in warmer areas may mate at any time of year. The male snake usually leaves afterward. About two-thirds of all female snakes lay eggs in a safe place and then leave. Baby snakes grow inside the eggs. Most of them have sharp teeth that they use to cut through the egg to hatch. Once a baby snake leaves the egg, it must face many dangers and survive on its own. Some female snakes hold their eggs inside their body until they hatch. Then they give birth to live babies.
pages.brief: A female snake lays eggs in a safe, hidden place and leaves them. Inside the eggs, baby snakes grow sharp teeth to cut through the shell. Nearby, another female holds eggs inside her body until they hatch, then gives birth to live babies.

pages.text: Venomous Snakes Venom is a dangerous substance. Venom comes from the fangs on a snake’s jaws. Venom is made in sacs behind a snake’s eyes. Some fangs are hollow so the venom can flow through them from these sacs.
pages.brief: A snake's head is shown with fangs on its jaws and venom sacs behind its eyes. Hollow fangs let venom flow from the sacs through the fangs. The snake holds its mouth slightly open, revealing the dangerous substance within.

pages.text: Snakes use venom to defend and attack. Snakes usually inject more venom when they are defending themselves. The venom paralyzes their prey. Some inject venom and let the prey go. Then they track the prey until it dies. Other snakes use their teeth or body to hold on to prey until it dies. Then they eat it. Venom versus Poison Although commonly confused, venom and poison are not the same thing. Poison is absorbed through the skin, eaten, or breathed in, while venom is injected into the victim by means of a bite or sting.
pages.brief: A snake bites to defend itself or attack prey, sending venom through its fangs. The venom paralyzes the prey, and a snake tracks the weakened animal until it dies. Another snake holds prey with its teeth and body until death. Venom is injected by a bite or sting, while poison is absorbed through skin, eaten, or breathed in.

pages.text: Conclusion Snakes are among the animal kingdom’s strongest hunters. They have survived in most places all over the world. Their senses have adapted to the natural world in many ways. Snakes are fascinating animals that play an important role in our environment.
pages.brief: Several snakes appear in different habitats, on land, in trees, and in water, showing how they have survived in most places. Their senses help them hunt. Together they represent the snake's role in the natural world and its place among the animal kingdom's strongest hunters.

books.title: Bison Came Back
books.art_why: The book includes 1800s hunting and early 1900s recovery, when photographs of these events are not available; drawn scenes suit the historical events.

pages.text: Great Beasts Bison are the biggest animals in North America. They weigh up to 2,000 pounds (907 kg)—almost half as much as a car. They can run 35 miles (56 km) per hour.
pages.brief: A huge bison stands on a North American grassland, its heavy body and shaggy coat showing why it is the biggest animal there. Another bison runs fast across the grass, strong and powerful, almost half as heavy as a car.

pages.text: Although they are big, fast, and strong, bison almost went extinct. People nearly wiped them out by hunting too many.
pages.brief: A large herd of big, fast, strong bison grazes on open land. Many hunters with rifles surround them, shooting too many, and the once-huge herd grows smaller. The animals are in danger of disappearing forever.

pages.text: People changed their ways just in time. They stopped the big hunts and protected land where bison live. Bison bounced back. Today, there are about a half million bison in North America. If you visit a place such as Yellowstone National Park, you can see them for yourself. Bison or Buffalo? North American settlers often called the shaggy beasts buffalo. Many people still do. In fact, buffalo are a different animal from bison. Buffalo live in Africa and Asia and have no hump. Their heads are smaller, too. However, “buffalo” has become a common name for bison in North America.
pages.brief: People stop the big hunts and set aside protected land where a bison herd has bounced back, while visitors watch from a distance. Nearby, a different buffalo from Africa or Asia stands with no hump and a smaller head.

pages.text: The Great Plains CANADA UNITED STATES MEXICO Millions Turns to Thousands Once, there were around thirty million bison in North America. They lived in large herds, mostly on the Great Plains.
pages.brief: A vast North American grassland stretches to the horizon, covered with enormous herds of bison. Thirty million animals move slowly together across the Great Plains, their dark backs packed close as they graze and travel.

pages.text: They were an important animal for many Native American people. Not only did bison provide food, but their hides were used for clothing and shelter. Native Americans also made bison bones into tools. They used all parts of a bison. For many years, Native Americans lived along with bison. They hunted what they needed but always left enough for herds to stay big.
pages.brief: Native American people live alongside a bison herd on the plains. A family uses bison hides for clothing and shelter, and makes tools from bones. They hunt only what they need, always leaving enough bison for the herds to stay big.

pages.text: As settlers moved into the western United States in the 1800s, more bison were hunted. Bison were often killed for sport or for their hides, which were sold. As railroads spread across the West, they brought more hunters. Sometimes thousands of bison were killed in a single day. The U.S. government also killed bison as a way to drive Native Americans off the land. Sadly, by 1889, there were only about one thousand bison left.
pages.brief: In the 1800s, settlers and hunters shoot bison from a passing railroad, killing them for sport and for hides to sell. Government hunters also kill bison to drive Native Americans off the land. By 1889, only about one thousand bison remain.

pages.text: New Help For years, few people did anything about the bison killing. Some bison were sent to zoos and ranches to protect them. Over time, laws were passed to protect bison in other places. Yellowstone National Park, formed in 1872, became a safe place for bison. People could not hunt them there.
pages.brief: Some bison are sent to zoos and ranches where they are protected. In Yellowstone National Park, formed in 1872, bison roam safe land where people cannot hunt them. Over time, new laws are passed to protect bison in other places too.

pages.text: In the early 1900s, people shipped bison from East Coast zoos back out West. In 1913, fourteen were brought by train from New York to Wind Cave National Park in South Dakota. Several hundred wild bison live on that land today.
pages.brief: People bring fourteen bison by train from New York to Wind Cave National Park in South Dakota in 1913. The animals arrive at the park. Today, several hundred wild bison live on that same land.

pages.text: By 1916, there were just twenty-three bison in Yellowstone, but people shipped more there, too. The bison had plenty of room to roam, and soon their numbers began to grow. Today, there are several thousand bison in Yellowstone.
pages.brief: By 1916, only twenty-three bison remain in Yellowstone. People ship more bison there, and the animals have plenty of room to roam. Soon their numbers begin to grow. Today, several thousand bison live in Yellowstone National Park.

pages.text: People in other places also helped bison bounce back. Bison live today on ranches, on the National Bison Range in Montana, and on other government land.
pages.brief: Bison live on ranches and on government land in other places, helped by people who want them to bounce back. A herd grazes on the National Bison Range in Montana, while another group stands together on a ranch.

pages.text: Wonderful Sights Like thousands of other wild animals, bison almost went extinct. There will probably never be as many bison as there once were, but at least they still exist.
pages.brief: A wild bison stands on open land, a wonderful sight that almost disappeared from the world. Like thousands of other wild animals, bison came close to extinction. There may never be as many as before, but at least these great beasts still exist.

pages.text: Today, bison are easy to spot at a place such as Yellowstone. They love to roll around in the dirt. Sometimes one lets out a great, loud snort. They swim across rivers and run across the land, wild and free. It’s a wonderful sight to see.
pages.brief: At Yellowstone today, a bison rolls in the dirt, sending up dust, while another lets out a great, loud snort. Nearby, bison swim across a river and run across the land, wild and free, a wonderful sight to see.

books.title: Hula: The Heartbeat of Hawai'i
books.art_why: The book covers ancient and historical Hawaiian life, so drawn scenes suit it better than photos.

pages.text: of The Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: A simple opening view that introduces Hawai‘i as the subject of the book, with a calm, open scene and no people, actions, or other objects added, making the setting wide, still, very quiet, and uncluttered.

pages.text: Coming to Hawai‘i The dancers are excited to begin. They have joined a hula school and have danced for many months. Soon, they hear the beat of a drum. Their hula teacher starts to chant in Hawaiian. Now the dancers move together. Their legs sway in rhythm, and their arms move in smooth gestures. At times, they chant along, adding their voices to the story. They are doing hula, a special kind of dance created by their ancestors. They are keeping hula alive today.
pages.brief: Excited dancers at a hula school hear a drum and their teacher chants in Hawaiian; the dancers move together, legs swaying in rhythm and arms making smooth gestures, and at times they chant along, adding their voices to the story of hula.

pages.text: Hawai‘i was settled by Polynesian people around 1200 ce. They traveled 2,600 miles (4,184 km) from the island of Tahiti in the South Pacific Ocean. For most of Hawai‘i’s history, its people did not have a written language. Instead, storytellers told tales with chants and songs. Music and dance added rhythm and drama to these stories. This helped Hawaiian people remember important events in their history. Hawai‘i is the only U.S. state that is made up entirely of islands. Each of its eight main islands was created by at least one volcano. Some traditional Hawaiian stories told about the volcanoes that created the islands. Hula: The Heartbeat of Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: Polynesian people travel from Tahiti across the ocean to settle in Hawai‘i around 1200 CE; storytellers chant and sing tales with music and dance, and volcanic islands rise in the background as traditional stories tell about the volcanoes that created them.

pages.text: Ancient Hula Traditional Hawaiian storytellers spoke of their ancestors. They told tales about love, war, and Hawaiian gods. They made up songs for important events. Dancers chanted along and danced, often using gestures that helped bring the stories to life. Together, these artists created ancient hula, or hula kahiko (HOO-lah kah-HEE-koh). Hula Skirts Traditionally, hula dancers did not wear grass skirts. Both men and women wore skirts or loincloths made from kapa cloth. Kapa cloth was made from tree bark.
pages.brief: Traditional Hawaiian storytellers and dancers perform ancient hula, chanting and using gestures to tell tales of love, war, and gods; men and women wear skirts or loincloths made from kapa cloth, not grass skirts, as they bring the stories to life.

pages.text: Hula Evolves Some modern experts believe that this special dance style started as simple swaying and chanting along with storytellers. In modern hula, most steps are done with knees slightly bent. This lets dancers sway their hips easily. The hips and feet keep the rhythm. The upper body stays straight, appearing to float above the swaying hips. Over time, dancers began to use their arms to make gestures. These gestures described the words in the songs or chants. The dancers’ feelings showed on their faces. Hula teachers taught their students that “the eyes follow the hands.” That way, the dancers became storytellers, too! Hula: The Heartbeat of Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: Modern hula dancers keep their knees slightly bent and sway their hips and feet to the rhythm while their upper bodies stay straight and appear to float; their arm gestures describe the song words, and their eyes follow their hands as their faces show feeling.

pages.text: In both ancient and modern hula, every part of the body dances. Hula dancers chant and also create other sounds that become part of the act. They jump, stomp, and slap the ground. These gestures add sound and rhythm to the dance. Hula Gestures.
pages.brief: In both ancient and modern hula, dancers use every part of their bodies, chanting and making other sounds as they jump, stomp, and slap the ground; these movements and gestures add sound and rhythm to the dance.

pages.text: The first people from Europe, led by the British explorer Captain James Cook, came to Hawai‘i in 1778. They didn’t stay, but they told the world about the islands. In the 1820s, white Christians from the United States came to Hawai‘i. They wanted Hawaiian people to stop practicing their traditional beliefs and become Christians, too. Because hula was a way to tell stories about Hawaiian gods, they thought it was wrong. The queen of Hawai‘i at the time became a Christian and banned hula in 1830. Then, hula could only be done in secret. Hula: The Heartbeat of Hawai‘i 10 Strangers Arrive For a while, hula was not allowed in Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: British explorer Captain James Cook and later white Christians from the United States arrive in Hawai‘i; the queen becomes Christian and bans traditional hula in 1830, so Hawaiian dancers practice hula quietly only in secret.

pages.text: King David For the next fifty years, hula was not allowed in Hawai‘i. King David, who ruled from 1874 to 1891, saw that the modern world was changing the country. As people came to Hawai‘i from other places, some Native Hawaiian people felt that their culture was being erased. King David wanted Hawaiian people to feel proud of their culture. He ignored the ban and invited hula dancers to his court. He said, “Hula is the language of the heart, therefore the heartbeat of the Hawaiian people.” King David was famous for his love of hula. During his rule, more than three hundred ancient hula chants and songs were written down and saved.
pages.brief: King David rules from 1874 to 1891 and invites hula dancers to his court, ignoring the ban; he loves hula and says it is the heartbeat of the Hawaiian people, and more than three hundred ancient chants and songs are written down and saved.

pages.text: Hard Times Although King David helped bring hula back to Hawaiian culture, its people would continue to face tough times. People from other lands brought new diseases that killed thousands of Native Hawaiian people. More than three hundred thousand Hawaiian people lived on the islands before 1780. By 1890, there were less than forty thousand. Then, in 1898, Hawai‘i became a U.S. territory. With the loss of so many people and the land itself, how could hula live on? Hula: The Heartbeat of Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: After King David’s help, Native Hawaiian people face hard times as new diseases kill thousands; the population falls from more than three hundred thousand before 1780 to less than forty thousand by 1890, and Hawai‘i becomes a U.S. territory in 1898.

pages.text: A New Style of Hula During the early 1900s, many new people came to Hawai‘i. They became interested in hula. A new, modern style of hula, called hula ‘auana (HOO-lah ow-AH-nah), was born. Hula ‘auana used Western- style music instead of chants. It also added new sounds such as the ukulele. ukulele.
pages.brief: In the early 1900s, new people come to Hawai‘i and become interested in hula; a modern style called hula ‘auana is born, using Western-style music instead of chants and adding new sounds such as the ukulele.

pages.text: Hula ‘auana songs still told stories but focused less on the meaning of the words than hula kahiko. Modern hula was more about the music and gestures, although the words and the dance were still connected. Hula: The Heartbeat of Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: Hula ‘auana dancers perform modern hula, which still tells stories but focuses less on the meaning of the words than hula kahiko; the music and gestures matter more, though the words and dance remain connected.

pages.text: Hawai‘i Reborn In 1959, Hawai‘i became the fiftieth U.S. state. The 1960s and 1970s marked a new interest in traditional Hawaiian culture. Hawaiian people wanted to bring back the culture that existed in Hawai‘i before people from other places arrived. Some people started studying the Hawaiian language. They learned about ancient hula chants and songs. They also learned to dance hula kahiko.
pages.brief: After Hawai‘i becomes the fiftieth U.S. state in 1959, the 1960s and 1970s bring new interest in traditional Hawaiian culture; people study the Hawaiian language and learn ancient hula chants, songs, and to dance hula kahiko.

pages.text: Today, the best hula dancers in the world go to Hawai‘i each spring. They gather to dance at a festival on the Big Island. The hula contest at the festival began in 1971. It is known as the “Olympics of Hula.” It has both hula kahiko and hula ‘auana contests to show how hula has changed over time. Many Native Hawaiian people—and others who care about Hawaiian culture—have started learning about hula again. This interest has helped the ancient stories of Hawai‘i stay alive. Hula lovers are making sure that the “heartbeat of the Hawaiian people” is still strong today. Hula: The Heartbeat of Hawai‘i.
pages.brief: Today the best hula dancers in the world gather each spring on the Big Island for a festival whose hula contest began in 1971; both hula kahiko and hula ‘auana contests show how hula has changed, and hula lovers keep ancient stories alive.

books.title: The Science of Hiccups
books.art_why: Hiccups, human bodies, animals and everyday children all exist in real life, so photographs fit.

pages.text: Hiccup Help You just finished lunch and—hic!— uh-oh. You drank a fizzy drink, and now— hic!—you have the hiccups! Your friends try to help. “Hold your breath!” says one. “Drink a glass of water upside down!” suggests another. “We have a spelling quiz today!” shouts a third.
pages.brief: A child sits at a lunch table with a fizzy drink, one hand pressed to their mouth mid-hiccup. Three friends lean in, each offering advice with eager faces and raised hands. Plates and cups are pushed aside on the table.

pages.text: “What?” you ask. “Not really,” your friend tells you. “I was just trying to scare the hiccups away!” You try a few tricks, but nothing works. Eventually, the hiccups go away on their own. Usually, hiccups are no big deal, and they come and go quickly. However, many people are curious about hiccups. Some have been trying for years to understand hiccups. They want to know what hiccups are, where they come from, and how to get rid of them. Do You Know? Some people are unlucky enough to have hiccups for months or even years! Jack O’Leary made headlines in 1956 when his hiccups ended after eight years. By that time, he had received more than one hundred thousand letters from people around the country suggesting cures.
pages.brief: One friend grins and makes a silly scary face, hands raised like a monster, while the hiccupping child looks surprised. Nearby, an older man sits surrounded by towering piles of letters and newspapers, a small smile on his face.

pages.text: What Are Hiccups? A hiccup is a muscle spasm, or twitch. The muscle that twitches is called the diaphragm. You use your diaphragm to breathe. Your diaphragm sits below your lungs and stretches across the bottom of your rib cage. Nerves carry signals from your brain to your diaphragm. To breathe in, your brain tells the diaphragm to tighten. When your diaphragm tightens, it moves downward, which pulls air into your lungs. When your brain tells your diaphragm to relax again, the muscle moves up to push air back out of your lungs.
pages.brief: A child sits upright with one hand flat just below the ribs, breathing in slowly. Their chest lifts. Another child watches and copies the same calm breathing, both seated side by side in a bright room.

pages.text: Breathing in Hiccupping Breathing out During a hiccup, your brain sends a signal to your diaphragm to suddenly jerk downward. Your diaphragm pulls a quick gasp of air into your lungs, and flaps in your throat slam shut. That is why you make a sudden “hic!” sound. Hiccups get their name from this sound.
pages.brief: A child freezes mid-breath, mouth open in a sudden jerk, eyes wide with surprise. One hand flies to the throat. A friend nearby turns to look, caught between concern and a smile.

pages.text: The spasm can be strong enough to make your whole body jerk. Sometimes, if you have a full stomach, it can even be painful. However, hiccups are not harmful. Take a Breath Have you ever heard of “getting the wind knocked out of you”? Your diaphragm is involved when this happens, too. If you get hit hard in the chest or back, your diaphragm can spasm for a few seconds. The spasm makes it hard to breathe. Soon, your diaphragm relaxes, and you can breathe again.
pages.brief: A child stands on a playground, body jerking with a hiccup, shoulders lifted and face tense. Nearby, another child bends forward after a ball hit their chest, one hand pressed to their ribs, breathless.

pages.text: What Causes Hiccups? Hiccups can seem to start for no reason. They might happen when you eat too much or too quickly. Many people get them from eating spicy foods or having fizzy drinks. We know some things about when people might get hiccups, however, we do not know exactly why people get them. Hiccups seem to have no purpose. Scientists have come up with a few theories, or ideas, though. Scientists have found that other animals get hiccups, too. Most that do are mammals. Mammals are animals that drink milk from their mother when they are young. Hiccups are more common in baby mammals, which could be a clue.
pages.brief: Children share spicy snacks and fizzy drinks at a table, one mid-hiccup with a hand at their mouth. A small puppy nearby hiccups too, body jolting slightly. Bowls and cans are scattered across the tabletop.

pages.text: Baby mammals, including baby humans, need help burping. A burp is how the body gets rid of extra air in the stomach. It can be hard for babies to burp while drinking their mother’s milk. Hiccups may be a way for young mammals to burp. Scientists got another idea from looking at amphibians. These animals include frogs, which breathe water when they are young and air when they are adults. At one stage of growth, amphibians have two different ways to breathe. They can use their lungs to breathe air, or they can breathe water through gills. Do You Know? Babies can even hiccup before they are born! Scientists think it happens as a baby’s lungs, diaphragm, and nerves develop and begin working.
pages.brief: A mother gently pats a baby's back to help it burp, both calm. In the background, a frog sits half in a pond, head above water. A pregnant woman rests a hand on her belly, smiling softly.

pages.text: When they breathe water, their brain has to send a signal so they don’t breathe water into their lungs. This is similar to the signal the human brain sends during a hiccup. Hiccups may be a sign that the brain is reminding itself how to breathe correctly. Scientists have not yet proven either of these theories. We may never know exactly what hiccups are for. They may not even have a real purpose—maybe they are simply an odd accident in our bodies.
pages.brief: A frog floats in shallow pond water, head and eyes above the surface, throat pulsing. Its legs drift below. A scientist kneels at the bank with a notebook, watching the frog closely but not touching it.

pages.text: How Do I Get Rid of Hiccups? Getting rid of hiccups is another mystery. Everyone seems to have his or her own hiccup cure. Sometimes they work, and sometimes they don’t. A hiccup cure that seemed to work last week may not work today. No one has found a cure that works all the time for everyone. However, the most common cures have a few things in common.
pages.brief: Several children try different hiccup cures in a classroom: one holds their breath with puffed cheeks, another sips water, a third hangs upside down from a chair. A teacher watches with folded arms and a puzzled smile.

pages.text: Some cures change your breathing pattern. For example, you might hold your breath or breathe into a paper bag. These methods build up a gas called carbon dioxide in your body. When you have too much carbon dioxide, your body works harder to breathe it out. Your brain tells the diaphragm to relax so it can get rid of the carbon dioxide.
pages.brief: A child breathes slowly into a small paper bag, shoulders relaxed, eyes focused. Another child holds their breath, cheeks round and face pink. An adult kneels beside them, one hand raised calmly, watching both.

pages.text: Other cures distract you. You might try a tricky task, like drinking water from the opposite side of the glass. When you try to breathe or swallow in a different way, the signals between your brain and diaphragm may get confused. Your body may “forget” to hiccup while it tries to do the task. Getting scared works the same way—you get distracted from hiccups. These kinds of hiccup cures may not work forever. Your body learns how to do the tricky task or doesn’t get scared so easily. It becomes harder to distract your brain.
pages.brief: A child tips a glass of water to drink from the far rim, water sloshing, face concentrated. Beside them, a friend jumps out with raised arms to scare them. Another child watches and laughs, hand over mouth.

pages.text: Unsolved Mystery Hiccups are harmless, but they can be annoying. People have always gotten hiccups, but they are still a scientific mystery. Maybe one day you will be the one to solve the mystery and discover the cure!
pages.brief: A child sits at a desk with a glass of water, a notebook and a pencil, chin in hand, thinking hard. Their face is calm but slightly annoyed. Soft light falls across the desk.

books.title: The Terry Fox Story
books.art_why: Terry Fox is a named real person, so the book uses cartoon-style biography art.

pages.text: The Terry Fox Story.
pages.brief: An opening title page shows a single painted portrait of Terry Fox as a young runner, shown from the chest up, looking steadily ahead. The background is plain, keeping the focus on his face and the story ahead.

pages.text: The The Terry Fox Story Story.
pages.brief: A second title page shows Terry Fox running alone along a long empty road, one leg a prosthetic, his arms pumping. The scene is simple and quiet, introducing the journey that the book will tell.

pages.text: A Journey Begins Terry Fox was born in 1958 in Winnipeg, Canada. As a young boy, he loved to play sports and games that went on for days. Terry was serious about finishing any project, no matter how long it took. As a child, he loved sports of all kinds. He played baseball and soccer with his little brother, Darrell, and his best friend, Doug Alward. Terry earned a spot on his eighth-grade basketball team, but it wasn’t easy. He was not very tall and not a very good player. Still, through lots of hard work, Terry made the team.
pages.brief: A young Terry Fox plays baseball and soccer in a Winnipeg park with his little brother Darrell and his best friend Doug Alward. Nearby, Terry practices basketball alone on an outdoor court, working hard to make his eighth-grade team despite being shorter than the other players.

pages.text: High School and Beyond Terry kept getting better at basketball while playing for his high school. In his senior year, he shared an Athlete of the Year award with his buddy Doug. Terry also got good grades in school. He wasn’t sure what he wanted to be in the future, but he knew he wanted to keep playing basketball. He went to college at Simon Fraser University, which had the best basketball team in British Columbia. Making the team would take more hard work, but that was just fine with Terry.
pages.brief: Terry, taller now, plays basketball for his high school team and stands with his friend Doug as they share an Athlete of the Year award. Later he arrives at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia, where the college basketball team practises on an indoor court.

pages.text: Things Crash Terry earned a spot on the team, but then his life started to change. In November of his first year at college, he crashed his car. Terry wasn’t hurt badly in the crash, but his knee felt sore. He didn’t tell anyone about the pain. He thought his knee was hurting from basketball practice. By late winter, however, he was limping. His mother took him to the doctor. The news was not what they expected. The source of Terry’s leg pain was a rare form of cancer. The cause was unknown, but Terry had a type of cancer that could spread quickly and be deadly.
pages.brief: Terry's car sits damaged after a crash on a winter road. At home, Terry limps across a room while his mother watches with concern, then sits in a doctor's office as the doctor explains that the pain in his leg comes from a rare cancer.

pages.text: What Is Cancer? Cancer is the name for a group of diseases that cause a person’s body cells to grow out of control. The disease can start almost anywhere—in bones or even blood. Then, cancer cells can spread throughout the body, creating lumps called tumors. Cancer is the second-leading cause of death around the world.
pages.brief: A clear illustration of the human body shows cells growing out of control inside a bone and in the blood, forming a lump called a tumor. The image compares healthy cells with cancer cells spreading through the body.

pages.text: Terry was angry and fearful when he first heard the news. He went through many different feelings as he began treatment. He moved into the hospital, and his right leg was removed above the knee. Doctors hoped this would keep the cancer from spreading. No one could say for sure, however, that the cancer wouldn’t return. Terry had to learn how to walk using a prosthetic leg. Months of cancer treatments followed. The treatments weakened his body and caused his hair to fall out. In the hospital, Terry met other people who were being treated for cancer. He realized their experiences were similar to his.
pages.brief: Terry sits on a hospital bed, his face angry and fearful, as doctors treat him. Later he learns to walk on a prosthetic leg in a hospital corridor, his hair gone from treatment, and he talks with other patients who are also being treated for cancer.

pages.text: An Athlete’s Life Terry discovered he could still play sports, though often in new ways. He played wheelchair basketball. To strengthen his body, he trained hard like he always had before. Next, Terry tried running, which was awkward at first with a prosthetic leg. Soon, however, he got the hang of it and began regular training. At his first race, Terry came in last. Still, he felt happy. He had learned that he could do the things he had always loved.
pages.brief: Terry plays wheelchair basketball on an indoor court, then trains hard with weights. Outside, he runs on a track with a prosthetic leg, his stride awkward at first, and finishes last in his first race, smiling as he crosses the line.

pages.text: A Plan Unfolds Like other cancer survivors, Terry hoped that his cancer would never return. He came up with a plan to help in the search for a cure for the disease. He decided to run across Canada. As he ran, people could give money for cancer research. A huge run such as this one was a lot to take on. But Terry knew that his idea could help a good cause and he carefully planned the trip. He would call his run the Marathon of Hope. His friend Doug would go along with him, driving a van. On April 12, 1980, the Marathon of Hope began in St. John’s, Newfoundland, in eastern Canada.
pages.brief: Terry stands beside a van at the eastern edge of Canada with his friend Doug, ready to begin the Marathon of Hope on April 12, 1980. The road ahead stretches far into the distance from St. John's, Newfoundland.

pages.text: Running Across Canada The run was hard from the start. The days were long, and the weather was freezing cold. At rest breaks, Terry and Doug huddled in the van, making snacks. The narrow country roads Terry ran on were dangerous to share with drivers. Every day Terry’s legs hurt, and he quickly grew sunburned. Sometimes, Terry showed up in a town exhausted, and no one was there to meet him. Other times, whole towns lined the streets to cheer him.
pages.brief: Terry runs along a narrow country road in freezing weather, his legs aching and his face sunburned. At a rest break, he and Doug huddle inside the van making snacks. In one town the street is empty; in another, crowds line the road cheering.

pages.text: Growing Support Terry crossed province after province, running the distance of a marathon each day. Each week of running was draining. Terry’s spirits were lifted when his younger brother, Darrell, joined him on the trip. Growing crowds also made him happy. By late June, dozens of television stations and newspapers were covering his run. The entire country began to follow his journey. In Toronto, Ontario, thousands of people lined the streets as he ran through the city. Money for cancer research was streaming in.
pages.brief: Terry runs through a Canadian town while crowds line the street and cheer. His younger brother Darrell runs beside him. Television cameras and newspaper reporters follow along, and in Toronto thousands of people fill the sidewalks as Terry passes through the city.

pages.text: Route of Marathon of Hope NORTH AMERICA Newfoundland Prince Edward Island Quebec Ontario Canada Nova Scotia United States Terrible News Then, on September 1, after 5,300 kilometers (3,300 mi.), the Marathon of Hope came to a sudden end. Terry had been feeling sick, and in Thunder Bay, Ontario, he stopped to visit doctors. They discovered that the cancer was back. Terry wanted to keep running, but it was impossible. He had to fly home to get care.
pages.brief: A map of eastern Canada shows the route of the Marathon of Hope across Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, Quebec and Ontario. In Thunder Bay, Terry sits in a doctor's office and learns the cancer has returned; later he boards a plane home.

pages.text: Terry’s death shocked and saddened many people across Canada and the world. A large crowd gathered for his funeral in Vancouver. Terry’s Race Goes On Terry got eight more months of treatment, but on June 28, 1981, he died. Although Terry never finished the Marathon of Hope, the run met his goals. Millions of people learned about the need to find cures for different types of cancer. Terry’s work to fund cancer research didn’t end with his death. Today, the Terry Fox Foundation continues to raise money. Terry’s story still helps new people learn about the cause.
pages.brief: A large crowd gathers for Terry's funeral in Vancouver, many people standing quietly with sad faces. Later, the Terry Fox Foundation office is shown with workers organizing fundraising materials, carrying Terry's cause forward after his death on June 28, 1981.

pages.text: Many people take part in yearly Terry Fox runs—one-day events that raise money for cancer research. These runs have taken place in Canada and countries all over the world. So far, the foundation has raised more than 800 million dollars to fund cancer research. A complete cure for cancer hasn’t been found yet, but huge progress has been made. Terry’s run helped people see the difference a single person can make in the world.
pages.brief: Many people take part in a yearly Terry Fox run, jogging together along a city street and through a park in Canada and other countries. Runners of all ages move together down the road, and the crowd stretches far into the distance.

books.title: How Memory Works
books.art_why: Real-world science, people, brains, and technology can be shown with photographs.

pages.text: How Memory Works.
pages.brief: An imaginative cover scene shows a human brain floating with softly glowing connected pathways and rippling patterns, suggesting memory and thought; a quiet, curious atmosphere surrounds the brain alone, with no people or objects nearby.

pages.text: A Quick Experiment Let’s do an experiment. Pay attention to what’s going on around you for just a moment. What can you see, touch, taste, smell, and hear? After you paid attention to your senses, did you notice anything different? You probably did. That’s because our brains are always receiving information from our senses. There is so much information, though, that we can’t possibly pay attention to all of it. Indeed, we only remember a very small amount of the information around us. How does memory work? Scientists have some ideas, but many more questions remain.
pages.brief: A child pauses in a bright room and pays close attention to the world around them, noticing what can be seen, touched, tasted, smelled, and heard; soft streams of sensory information drift toward the child’s brain.

pages.text: Types of Memory Scientists often talk about two types of memory: working memory and long-term memory. Working memory is how we deal with information in the moment. The words you’re reading right now and the conversation you just had with a friend are part of your working memory. So is the music you were listening to on the way to school. We use our working memory most of the time.
pages.brief: A child reads a book in class, chats with a friend, and wears headphones on the way to school, showing everyday moments held in working memory; nearby, a long-term memory glows as a distant, lasting pattern.

pages.text: Short-term memories make up our working memory, which also includes something called executive attention. This is the process of how our brains filter information into short-term memory. Think about the experiment at the beginning of this book. Even when we’re sitting quietly, our brains can’t handle all the information we receive. Our brains ignore most of the information around us to keep from overloading. The information we do keep in our minds at any one time makes up our short-term memory. Most of us can only hold around three to four thoughts in our short-term memory at once.
pages.brief: A child sits quietly as many sights and sounds press in; a glowing brain filters most of them away, keeping only a few thoughts. Three or four small glowing thought shapes remain in the foreground.

pages.text: For example, you might be listening to your teacher and scratching an itch on your arm at the same time. You might think about a few other ideas. Then someone sneezes loudly. What happens? Your attention turns to the person who sneezed. Information only stays in our short- term memory for a few seconds. Once our executive attention gets to work and we start paying attention to something, things change. Our executive attention makes sure that unimportant information doesn’t interrupt the things that we are concentrating on. It also makes sure we pay attention to other important things, such as a sneeze. Your brain may think any loud, sudden noise means danger. If we don’t give information attention, it leaves our memory. The more we pay attention to something, the better chance we have to remember it.
pages.brief: In a classroom, a child listens to the teacher while scratching an itch on an arm, then turns as another student sneezes loudly; the sudden, sharp sound grabs the child’s attention away from the lesson.

pages.text: Long-term memories function differently from working memories. They remain in our minds even when we’re not thinking about them. Scientists think information has to go through three steps to become a long- term memory. First, we learn something. Then, we store it. Later, we retrieve it. We can bring back long-term memories when needed. For example, think about your birthday. The date probably came to mind before you even finished reading the sentence. Maybe other memories, such as your birthday parties, also came to mind. You might have even thought about your family. That’s because our brains connect different pieces of related information.
pages.brief: A child pauses in a warm room as a birthday date comes clearly to mind; nearby, bright scenes of a birthday party and family appear, showing related long-term memories connecting, storing, and returning when needed.

pages.text: Memory and the Brain Our brains do not process or store memories in a single area. In fact, we often use many parts of our brains to make and keep memories. New technology lets scientists see what parts of the brain become active when we use different kinds of memory. The hippocampus (hih-puh-KAM-puhss) is an important part of the brain concerning memory. People have two hippocampi—one on each side of their brain. Scientists aren’t exactly sure how hippocampi work, but they turn short-term memories into long-term memories. They also help us retrieve long-term memories. I Remember Everything! Can you remember everything you did yesterday? What about what you were doing on November 7 two years ago? Some people can remember everything. They recall what they did and who they were with for almost every day of their life— even as babies. Can you remember everything you did yesterday? What about what you were doing on November 7 two years ago? Some people can remember everything. They recall what they did and who they were with for almost every day of their life— even as babies.
