pages.brief: Scientists study glowing brain images in a lab, showing several active areas; a central brain reveals two small curved regions, one on each side. Nearby, a person sits quietly, recalling many past days and people.

pages.text: Unlocking the Mysteries of the Brain Scientists learned a lot about what the hippocampus does through working with a patient, Henry Molaison (MOH-luh- suhn), known as HM. He was born with a disease called epilepsy (EH-puh-lep-see), which affects the brain. Doctors removed part of HM’s brain, including the hippocampus, when he was twenty-seven to try to help him. He got better, but he was no longer able to form some types of long-term memories. For example, HM could learn new motor skills, such as drawing a star in a mirror or walking with crutches. However, he couldn’t remember someone he met minutes before, new words, or songs. In fact, he couldn’t remember any new information about himself or his experiences after the age of sixteen. Scientists studied HM for fifty-five years before he died in 2008. Much of what we know about how memory works is thanks to studies done with him. In fact, HM is one of the most studied people in the history of medicine!
pages.brief: A historical clinic portrait shows Henry Molaison as an adult, with doctors studying his brain; inset scenes show him drawing a star in a mirror and using crutches, while new faces, words, and songs fade away.

pages.text: Other parts of our brain become active with muscle memory. We form muscle memory when we repeat a movement over and over again. Eventually, we don’t even have to think about how to do the movement—we just do it.
pages.brief: A child practices the same action again and again in a bright practice room, then performs it smoothly and easily without thinking hard; the repeated movement becomes automatic, showing muscle memory forming through steady practice.

pages.text: Losing Memory Damage to the brain can cause people to lose their memory. This is called amnesia. They may forget just a few minutes or a long period of time. It depends on how bad the damage is. Sometimes amnesia goes away in days, weeks, or months. Other times, it never goes away. One of the most common diseases that affects memory is called Alzheimer’s (AHLTS-hy-murz). People who have Alzheimer’s lose their memories over time. Most of the people who have the disease are over the age of sixty-five. Scientists don’t know what causes Alzheimer’s. Another part of our brain connects feelings to memory. Strong feelings, such as happiness, sadness, or pride, can make memories last longer. They help make memories clearer. While people remember happy memories, they often recall painful or sad memories more clearly —especially ones they’d rather forget.
pages.brief: An older adult sits alone, looking uncertain and showing memory loss; a soft image of a damaged brain appears nearby, alongside two strong memories, one happy and one painful, glowing clearly in the quiet room.

pages.text: Improving Memory Information enters our long-term memory in a few different ways. One way is to repeat something over time. The more you experience something, the better you remember it. It’s also true that the longer the period of time over which you repeat something, the better you’ll remember it. This is why studying every day helps you do better in school. You’ll remember more if you study for one hour a day for five days than five hours in one day.
pages.brief: A student studies at a desk in five short daily sessions, then contrasts this with one long, tiring study session; steady repetition across days looks calm and effective, showing better remembering in a bright room.

pages.text: You can also learn by using mnemonic (nih-MON-ik) devices that help you remember information. They connect new information to information you already know or that is easy to remember. One example is “Never eat soggy waffles.” People use this sentence to remember the names and order of the four major directions. The first letter of each word is the same as the first letter of north, south, east, and west. You still need to repeat mnemonic devices over and over to remember the connection. However, they help you remember more with less work. Give it a try! ever North at affles East West South oggy.
pages.brief: A child grins at a plate of soggy waffles, with four compass directions softly arranged around the bright scene, linking the funny phrase to north, south, east, and west in a playful, very memorable moment.

pages.text: Mysterious Memory We learn more about memory every year. New technology helps scientists study our brains in action. Yet scientists still don’t really know what memories are or how they are made. They also don’t know how memories move from our working memory to our long-term memory. How we retrieve them is also a mystery. Scientists have ideas about how memory works, but it could be many years before we have clear answers to these mysteries. Whoever discovers how memory works will be remembered far into the future. Could it be you?
pages.brief: Scientists use modern scanning equipment to watch a brain clearly at work, while a young, curious child looks on beside them, imagining new future discoveries about memory, mystery, and the brain in a bright laboratory.

books.title: Mysterious Mars
books.art_why: The book covers ancient sightings, 1800s astronomers and early space missions, so drawn scenes fit better than photos.

pages.text: Introduction Long ago, ancient people saw a bright red light in the sky. The Romans named this red light Mars, after their god of war. The name stuck, and we still use it today for the fourth planet in our solar system.
pages.brief: Ancient people stand outdoors at night, looking up at a bright red light in the sky. Roman figures in robes and armor look toward the glowing planet, and a stern warrior god figure stands nearby as the name Mars is chosen.

pages.text: Gazing from Afar Ancient astronomers wondered what made Mars red. Astronomers in the 1800s studied the planet through early telescopes. They found that Mars had polar ice caps just as Earth did. Parts of Mars were also covered with long lines that looked like a web of waterways.
pages.brief: Astronomers in 1800s clothing peer through early telescopes at Mars, which hangs in the dark sky. On the planet's surface, white polar ice caps and long lines spread like a web of waterways.

pages.text: An Italian astronomer who discovered these lines in 1877 called them channels. Channels are natural waterways. People thought the astronomer said he saw canals. Canals are waterways built by people. The mix-up led people to believe that intelligent beings built canals on Mars! Were the channels on Mars really canals? Had they held water? And why was Mars red? Scientists had many questions about the planet.
pages.brief: An Italian astronomer at a telescope in 1877 studies the long lines on Mars. Nearby, people imagine intelligent beings building canals across the planet, while natural channels and human-built canals are shown as different ideas.

pages.text: Taking a Closer Look In the 1960s, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) began the Mariner missions to answer these questions. The Mariner 4 spacecraft traveled to Mars to take close-up pictures. The pictures showed that the “canals” were canyons.
pages.brief: A Mariner 4 spacecraft flies through dark space toward Mars in the 1960s, carrying cameras to take close-up pictures. The images reveal that the long lines on the Martian surface are deep canyons, not canals.

pages.text: The Mariner 9 spacecraft showed that Mars had valleys and volcanoes. One of the volcanoes is the largest on any planet in our solar system. It is 26 kilometers (16 mi.) high and 500 kilometers (311 mi.) wide at its base. That’s three times as tall as Mount Everest! Mariner 9 was launched in 1971. It was the first satellite to orbit Mars, and it stayed in orbit for nearly a year. During that time, it collected over seven thousand images, which allowed scientists to map most of the Martian surface.
pages.brief: The Mariner 9 spacecraft orbits Mars in 1971, gathering thousands of images. Below, a giant volcano rises from the Martian surface, far taller than Mount Everest, and long, deep valleys stretch across the planet.

pages.text: Earth 365 days Mars Why is a Mars year almost twice as long as an Earth year? A year is the amount of time it takes a planet to orbit the Sun. Mars is farther away from the Sun than Earth is, so it has a longer distance to travel. Its orbiting speed is also a bit slower than Earth’s. Scientists also learned that the atmosphere on Mars is much thinner than Earth’s. It can’t filter the Sun’s harmful rays the way Earth’s atmosphere can. Mars is also very cold, with an average temperature of −63 ° Celsius (−81 ° F).
pages.brief: Earth and Mars travel around the Sun, with Mars on a longer, slower orbit. A thin atmosphere surrounds Mars, offering little protection from the Sun's rays, while the planet's cold surface lies under a harsh sky.

pages.text: Mars is much smaller than Earth, so why is the amount of land surface of these planets nearly the same? Take a look at the picture of Earth below. See all that blue? Most of the Earth’s surface is covered by water. Mars is a desert planet. Its surface is not covered by water. Mars Earth This helped explain why the surface of Mars is so dry. Water freezes or evaporates in the dry, cold air of Mars. The dry soil and lack of water cause heavy dust storms on large areas of the planet. Martian Moons The two Martian moons are called Phobos (FOH-bohs) and Deimos (DEE-mohs). These are Greek words meaning “fear” and “panic.” Phobos and Deimos were the twin sons of the Greek god of war, Ares. Deimos Phobos.
pages.brief: Earth appears mostly blue with oceans, while Mars is a dry desert planet with no water covering its surface. Dust storms sweep across Martian land, and two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, circle the planet.

pages.text: Viking The 1976 Viking mission was made up of two spacecraft. It was the first mission to land on the surface of Mars. Both spacecraft looked for signs of life by testing soil samples. In 1976, the Viking 2 rover landed on Mars and took samples of the surface. It sent information back to scientists on Earth. The scientists learned that the rusty red color was due to large amounts of iron, a metal, in the soil. Viking also reported no signs of organic matter—the remains of living things. Mars seemed to be a dry, desert planet.
pages.brief: In 1976, the Viking spacecraft arrive at Mars, and Viking 2 lands on the surface. It takes soil samples and sends information back to scientists on Earth, who learn the rusty red soil contains iron and no organic matter.

pages.text: Would I be weightless on Mars? No, but you would weigh less because you would experience less than half the gravity you do on Earth. Scientists were still puzzled, though. Canyons on Earth are formed by running water. Mars looked like Earth without water. In 1997, the Mars Pathfinder also found rocks that seemed to have been shaped by water. Could Mars have had water long ago?
pages.brief: A person on Mars feels lighter than on Earth because of weaker gravity. Nearby, the Mars Pathfinder studies rocks that look shaped by water, while deep canyons on Earth show how running water carves rock.

pages.text: Curiosity Curiosity Curiosity, a car-sized rover, launched in 2011. Its mission was to see if Mars could have supported small life- forms called microbes, and if humans could survive there someday! Looking for Answers In 2003, the European Space Agency (ESA) launched the Mars Express. This spacecraft would orbit Mars and collect information about the planet. Just one month after arriving at Mars, Mars Express found ice at the planet’s south pole. This meant there was water on Mars.
pages.brief: A car-sized Curiosity rover explores Mars, searching for signs that microbes could have lived there and whether humans could survive. Above the planet, the Mars Express spacecraft orbits and finds ice at the south pole.

pages.text: How long is a day on Mars? A Martian day is just a bit longer than an Earth day—24 hours and 37 minutes. For the next several years, the Mars Express studied the planet’s south pole. In July 2018, European scientists said they had found a saltwater lake underneath about 2 kilometers (1 mi.) of ice on the surface of Mars. They think this lake is 20 kilometers (12 mi.) wide. Scientists think there may be other lakes, too, that might even contain life. In 2012 NASA sent the Curiosity rover to Mars. Curiosity tested samples of the soil and air on Mars. The air samples contained a gas called methane. On Earth, tiny living things called microbes make methane. Scientists wondered if the same might be true on Mars.
pages.brief: Under a thick layer of ice at Mars's south pole, scientists find a wide saltwater lake. Nearby, the Curiosity rover tests soil and air, finding methane gas that on Earth is made by tiny living things.

pages.text: Scientists can’t say for sure if life really did or does exist on Mars. More Mars missions are planned for 2020 and beyond. These missions will send rovers to look for signs of life. They will also gather information to see if it might be possible for people to someday live there. Perhaps one day, Mars will be inhabited by intelligent beings—from Earth!
pages.brief: Scientists on Earth study Mars with future rovers, still unsure whether life ever existed there. They plan more missions to look for signs of life and to learn whether people could someday live on the red planet.
